questions.text: An e-commerce company wants to group customers based on purchasing behavior without predefined labels. Which method should be used?

feedback.right: No predefined labels means unsupervised learning, and clustering groups customers who behave alike.
feedback.wrong: No labels means unsupervised learning, so it's clustering. Linear and logistic regression both need a known target value to learn from.

questions.text: A company uses a text-generation GenAI model for product descriptions, and the results are based on inputs provided in the input box.  What is this technique called?

feedback.right: The output is steered purely by the text you give the model. That's prompt engineering; the model itself never changes.
feedback.wrong: It's prompt engineering: only the input text shapes the result. Model tuning would change the model's weights, which isn't happening here.

questions.text: A developer is designing a function that should not unintentionally modify data outside its scope. To ensure the function does not produce side effects, which type of objects should be passed to the function?

feedback.right: Immutable objects (ints, strings, tuples) can't be changed in place, so the function can't alter the caller's data.
feedback.wrong: Pass immutable objects. A function can change a mutable argument like a list or dict in place, and the caller will see that change.

questions.text:
A programmer runs the following loop to display numbers:
```
for i in range(3):
    print(i)
```
What will be the output?

feedback.right: range(3) starts at 0 and stops before 3, giving 0, 1, 2.
feedback.wrong: range(3) yields 0, 1, 2. It starts at 0 and the stop value 3 is never included.

questions.text: A Spark aggregation by city runs very slowly due to skew. What is the best solution?

feedback.right: Salting adds a random suffix to hot keys so one heavy city is split across many tasks, then the partial results are combined.
feedback.wrong: Use salting. Skew means a few keys hold most rows; a random salt on those keys spreads them out. More memory or a random repartition still sends each key to one task.

questions.text: You are analyzing website traffic data over several months. You want to identify trends or seasonal patterns. Which visualization is most appropriate?

feedback.right: Line charts plot values over time, which makes trends and seasonal cycles easy to spot.
feedback.wrong: A line chart shows change over time. Histograms and box plots show distributions, and pie charts show parts of a whole, so none of them show a trend.

questions.text: A React component re-renders infinitely after an API call. What would be the root cause of this?

feedback.right: If the effect sets state it also depends on (or has no dependency array), each update re-runs the fetch, forever.
feedback.wrong: The usual cause is a wrong useEffect dependency: the effect updates state that's also in its dependency list, so every render fetches again. A missing key only causes a warning.

questions.text: What is the output of for i in 1 2 3; do echo $i; done?
options: Each number on a new line

feedback.right: echo adds a newline every time it runs, so 1, 2 and 3 land on separate lines.
feedback.wrong: echo ends its output with a newline and runs once per value, so you get 1, 2 and 3 on three separate lines.

questions.text: An email service automatically sorts messages into spam and non-spam categories. What type of Machine Learning problem can be used here?

feedback.right: Spam or not-spam is a fixed set of labels, which makes it (binary) classification.
feedback.wrong: It's classification: each email gets one of two labels. Regression predicts a number, and clustering finds groups without labels.

questions.text: Main disadvantage of circuit switching:

feedback.right: A circuit stays reserved for the whole call, even during silence, so that capacity sits idle.
feedback.wrong: The weakness is wasted bandwidth: the circuit is held for the whole call even when nobody is talking. Voice quality on circuit-switched lines is actually good.

questions.text:
Which condition should replace the blank so that the list comprehension selects even values from range(5)?
```
result = [x for x in range(5) if ____]
```

feedback.right: x % 2 is the remainder after dividing by 2, and it's 0 for even numbers.
feedback.wrong: Use x % 2 == 0, since even numbers leave no remainder. x < 0 matches nothing in range(5), and x == 0 keeps only 0.

questions.text:
While exploring data types, you notice that a numeric column is stored as text.
What type of issue is this during Exploratory Data Analysis?

feedback.right: Numbers stored as text are a type inconsistency. Convert them (for example with pd.to_numeric) before doing any maths.
feedback.wrong: It's a data type inconsistency: the values are numbers but the column type is text, so sums and comparisons break until you convert it.

questions.text: Which protocol is used for VoIP in packet networks?

feedback.right: SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) sets up, manages and ends VoIP calls.
feedback.wrong: It's SIP, which sets up and tears down VoIP calls. SS7, ISDN and TDM belong to the traditional circuit-switched phone network.

questions.text: You are running an async FastAPI application that works well during development but shows significant performance degradation under heavy load in production. CPU usage is low, yet requests are slow to complete. What is the most likely cause of this performance issue?

feedback.right: A blocking call (requests, time.sleep) inside async def freezes the event loop, so every request waits even though the CPU is idle.
feedback.wrong: Low CPU with slow requests points to blocking I/O inside async code. It stalls the single event loop; use an async client or run the call in a thread pool.

questions.text: Fault management primarily deals with:

feedback.right: Fault management is about detecting, logging and clearing alarms raised by network elements.
feedback.wrong: Fault management deals with alarms: detecting, correlating and clearing faults in the network. Coding, RF tuning and SIM making belong to other teams.

questions.text: What differentiates Generative AI from traditional ML models?
options: It can generate new content based on the data it was trained on

feedback.right: Generative models produce new content (text, images, code) that resembles what they were trained on.
feedback.wrong: The difference is that GenAI creates new content. Traditional ML mostly predicts a label or a number; GenAI writes text, images or code.

questions.text:
A user prompts GenAI recent event response chatbot , but the chatbot provided unrelated response.
What type of GenAI issue does this scenario illustrate?

feedback.right: A confident but unrelated or made-up reply is a hallucination, which is common when the model lacks recent information.
feedback.wrong: This is hallucination: the reply isn't grounded in facts. Overfitting, underfitting and data leakage are training problems, not chatbot output problems.

questions.text: What is the output of the following shell script?x="10"if [ $x -gt 5 ]; then echo "Yes"; else echo "No"; fi

feedback.right: 10 -gt 5 is true, so the then branch prints Yes.
feedback.wrong: It prints Yes. -gt compares numbers, 10 is greater than 5, so the then branch runs.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of supervised learning?
options: Predicting house prices using labeled data

feedback.right: Past sales give known prices, so the data is labeled. That makes it supervised learning (regression).
feedback.wrong: Supervised learning needs labeled data, as in predicting house prices from past sales. Grouping customers and finding hidden patterns are unsupervised.

questions.text: A software application is running in a production environment where monitoring, debugging, and log management are critical. Which approach represents the best logging practice for such a production application?

feedback.right: The logging module gives you levels, timestamps, handlers and formats, which production monitoring depends on.
feedback.wrong: Use Python's logging module. print and plain stdout have no levels or timestamps, and a custom logger rebuilds what logging already does.

questions.text: What does the command below do?cat file.txt | wc -l

feedback.right: wc -l counts lines, so this prints how many lines file.txt has.
feedback.wrong: wc -l counts lines; cat just feeds the file in. Counting only matching lines would need grep -c.

questions.text: When Form inputs behave inconsistently across renders. What would be the root cause?

feedback.right: An input that flips between controlled (value set) and uncontrolled (value undefined) behaves unpredictably, and React warns about it.
feedback.wrong: The cause is mixing controlled and uncontrolled inputs, often when value starts as undefined. Give state an initial value such as an empty string so the input stays controlled.

questions.text: You need to read data from a file in Python and make sure system resources are released properly, even if an exception occurs during processing, to avoid memory or resource issues later. Which approach should you use to read the file?

feedback.right: with open() closes the file automatically, even when an exception is raised.
feedback.wrong: Use with open(). The context manager closes the file even after an error. try-finally also works but is longer and easier to get wrong.

questions.text:
A developer is writing a function that adds two numbers and sends the result back to the caller. Which statement should be used to correctly complete the function?
```
def add(a,b): ____
```

feedback.right: return hands the value back to the caller, whereas print only shows it on screen.
feedback.wrong: Use return a+b. print just displays the sum and the function still returns None; yield would turn it into a generator.

questions.text: PSTN primarily uses which switching method?

feedback.right: The PSTN sets up a dedicated circuit for each call.
feedback.wrong: The PSTN uses circuit switching, a dedicated path per call. Packet switching is what the internet and VoIP use.

questions.text:
If the key "key" is not present in the dictionary data, what should be used as the default value in the code below?
```
value = data.get("key", ____)
```

feedback.right: None is the usual way to say 'no value', and it's also what get() returns when you don't pass a default.
feedback.wrong: The conventional default is None, which is also what get() returns if you leave the default out. KeyError is an exception, not a value.

questions.text: In LTE Which layer handles modulation and coding?

feedback.right: The physical layer handles modulation, coding and the radio signal itself.
feedback.wrong: Modulation and coding happen at PHY. MAC handles scheduling, RLC handles segmentation and retransmission, and RRC handles control signaling.

questions.text: While we are rendering 5,000 or more items there would be an UI lag. How can we optimize this?

feedback.right: Virtualization renders only the rows on screen, and memo stops unchanged rows from re-rendering.
feedback.wrong: Use memo plus virtualization (react-window, for example) so only visible rows are rendered. Redux or class components don't reduce the number of DOM nodes.

questions.text: A developer notices that a Spark job is taking longer than expected, even though the transformations used are very simple. What is the most likely reason for this behavior?

feedback.right: Transformations only build a plan. The work runs at an action such as count() or collect(), so that's where the time shows up.
feedback.wrong: Spark is lazy: transformations just record a plan, and everything runs at the first action. That's why the time appears there, not at the simple transformations.

questions.text: You are building a feature that needs to frequently check whether a value exists in a collection containing thousands of elements. Performance is critical. Which data structure is most efficient for fast membership checks in Python?

feedback.right: Sets are hash-based, so a membership check is O(1) on average.
feedback.wrong: Use a set. Its membership checks are O(1) on average thanks to hashing, while lists and tuples scan every element (O(n)).

questions.text:
A team wants testing activities to start parallel with development.
Which SDLC model supports this?

feedback.right: The V-Model pairs every development phase with a test phase that is planned at the same time.
feedback.wrong: It's the V-Model, which pairs each development phase with a test phase. Waterfall leaves testing until the build is finished.

questions.text:
A developer wants to search for the word "error" inside a log file.
Which command should be used?

feedback.right: grep searches text inside files, for example grep "error" app.log.
feedback.wrong: Use grep to search inside a file. find and locate look for files by name, not for text inside them.

questions.text:
A script needs to store temporary values only inside the script execution.
Which variable type should be used?

feedback.right: A local variable exists only while the script or function runs and disappears afterwards.
feedback.wrong: Use a local variable. Environment and exported variables get passed on to child processes, which temporary values don't need.

questions.text:
A developer wants to reuse a set of commands multiple times in a script.
What should they implement?

feedback.right: A function groups commands under a name, so you can call it as many times as you like.
feedback.wrong: Write a function: it bundles commands under a name you can call again. A loop repeats code in one spot but can't be called from elsewhere.

questions.text:
What does the following command do?
cat file.txt

feedback.right: cat prints a file's contents to the terminal.
feedback.wrong: cat displays a file's contents. Deleting is rm, renaming is mv and copying is cp.


questions.text: Which command is used to list files in a directory?

feedback.right: ls lists the contents of a directory.
feedback.wrong: On Linux it's ls. dir is the Windows command, and list and show aren't standard commands.

questions.text: Which symbol is used to define a variable in a shell script?

feedback.right: Assignment is name=value with no spaces. The $ is only for reading the value.
feedback.wrong: Write name=value, with no $ and no spaces around the =. The $ is only used to read a variable, as in echo $name.

questions.text: Which SDLC model follows a sequential approach where each phase must be completed before the next begins?

feedback.right: Waterfall runs each phase to completion before the next one starts.
feedback.wrong: That's Waterfall: requirements, design, build, test and deploy, each finished before the next. Agile and Spiral work in repeated cycles.

questions.text: Which shell is the default shell in most Linux systems today?

feedback.right: Bash (the Bourne Again Shell) is the default on most Linux distributions.
feedback.wrong: Bash is the default on most Linux distributions. The Bourne shell came before it, and C shell and Korn shell are alternatives.

questions.text: Which operator is used for numeric equality comparison in shell scripting?

feedback.right: -eq compares numbers, while = compares strings.
feedback.wrong: Use -eq for numbers inside [ ]. = and == compare strings, and === doesn't exist in shell.

questions.text:
What will be printed? for i in 1 2 3
```
do
echo $i
done
```

feedback.right: The loop echoes 1, 2 and 3 in order, one per line.
feedback.wrong: The loop prints 1, then 2, then 3, each on its own line. 123 would need echo -n, and nothing reverses the order.

questions.text: Which special variable represents all arguments passed to a script as separate strings?

feedback.right: "$@" expands to every argument as a separate word, so arguments containing spaces stay intact.
feedback.wrong: It's $@: all arguments, each as a separate string. $1 is only the first argument, $# is the count and $? is the last exit status.

questions.text: Which command is used to display the current working directory?

feedback.right: pwd stands for print working directory.
feedback.wrong: Use pwd. ls lists files, cd changes directory and whoami prints your username.

questions.text:
A script should execute different blocks of code based on multiple values of a variable.
Which structure should be used?

feedback.right: case matches one variable against many patterns, which is cleaner than a long if/elif chain.
feedback.wrong: Use case: it checks one variable against several values in one tidy block. if/elif works but gets messy with many values.

questions.text:
A developer wants to create a new directory called project_files.
Which command should be used?

feedback.right: mkdir creates a directory.
feedback.wrong: The command is mkdir project_files. create and newdir don't exist, and dir lists files.

questions.text: What is the primary goal of the Requirement Phase in SDLC?

feedback.right: The requirements phase pins down what users need before any design or code begins.
feedback.wrong: The requirements phase is about understanding what users need. Coding, testing and deployment come in later phases.

questions.text:
What will this script output?
```
function greet(){
echo "Welcome"
}
greet
```

feedback.right: Calling greet runs the function body, which echoes Welcome.
feedback.wrong: It prints Welcome. The function is defined first and then called by name, which runs its echo.

questions.text:
A script should repeat an operation until a user enters "exit".
Which loop is best suited?

feedback.right: A while loop keeps going while the input isn't exit, e.g. while [ "$input" != "exit" ].
feedback.wrong: The expected answer is a while loop that runs until the input is exit. An until loop can do it with the condition flipped, but while is the standard pick; for loops walk a known list.

What is the output?
```
a=5
b=3
echo $((a+b))
```

feedback.right: $(( )) evaluates arithmetic, so 5 + 3 gives 8.
feedback.wrong: It prints 8 because $(( )) does arithmetic. 53 would be string joining, which isn't what $(( )) does.

questions.text:
A company wants to release software quickly in multiple iterations with customer feedback.
Which model is suitable?

feedback.right: Agile delivers in short iterations and folds customer feedback into each one.
feedback.wrong: Agile fits: short iterations, frequent releases and feedback after each one. Waterfall and V-Model deliver once at the end.

questions.text:
A script should check whether a number is greater than 10.
Which condition is correct?

feedback.right: Inside [ ], -gt is the numeric 'greater than' test.
feedback.wrong: Use -gt. Inside [ ], > is treated as output redirection and creates a file named 10; gt without the dash isn't an operator.

questions.text:
A developer wants to redirect script output to a file.
Which operator is used?

feedback.right: > sends output to a file and overwrites it; >> appends instead.
feedback.wrong: Use > to send output to a file (>> appends). < reads input from a file, | passes output to another command and & runs it in the background.

questions.text:
What does this script do?
```
count=1
while [ $count -le 3 ]
do
echo $count ((count++))
done
```

feedback.right: count starts at 1, is printed, then incremented, and the loop stops once count passes 3.
feedback.wrong: It prints 1, 2, 3. ((count++)) raises count each pass, so the loop ends when count reaches 4 and the test -le 3 fails.

questions.text:
```
numbers = [1,2,2,3,3,4]
result = list(set(numbers))
print(result)
```

Which statement is TRUE?
options: Output contains unique values, but order is not guaranteed.

feedback.right: A set removes duplicates but has no guaranteed order, so the list you get back may not keep the original order.
feedback.wrong: A set removes duplicates but promises no order. Small ints often come out sorted in CPython, but that's an implementation detail you can't rely on.

questions.text: Why do scripts use if __name__ == "__main__":?
options: Without it, the file cannot be imported by other modules
It marks which function Python must execute first
It runs the guarded code only on direct execution, not on import
It declares the module as the root of the package

feedback.right: __name__ is "__main__" only when the file is run directly, so the guarded code is skipped on import.
feedback.wrong: The guard runs code only when the file is executed directly. When imported, __name__ is the module name, so that block is skipped. Files import fine without it.

questions.text: Which import statement imports only the sqrt function from the math module?

feedback.right: from module import name brings in just that one name.
feedback.wrong: Use from math import sqrt. import math.sqrt fails because sqrt is a function, not a submodule.

questions.text:
A class Car already has a method named start(). Another class ElectricCar(Car) defines its own start() method.
Which OOP concept is demonstrated?

feedback.right: A subclass redefining a parent method with the same name is method overriding.
feedback.wrong: It's method overriding: the subclass replaces the parent's start(). Overloading means same name with different parameters, which Python doesn't support directly.

questions.text:
A project contains the following structure:
project/
app.py
utils.py
Which statement imports the calculate() function from utils.py?

feedback.right: The module is named after the file (utils), and you import calculate from it.
feedback.wrong: Use from utils import calculate. import utils.calculate fails because calculate is a function, not a submodule.

Python

```
    print(file.readline())
```

feedback.wrong: It prints 2, then an empty line. readlines() already moved to the end of the file, so readline() has nothing left and returns ''.

questions.text: Which OOP concept allows a child class to use methods from its parent class?

feedback.right: Inheritance lets a child class reuse the parent's methods without rewriting them.
feedback.wrong: That's inheritance: the child class gets the parent's methods for free. Polymorphism is about the same call behaving differently on different classes.

questions.text:
A developer wants to reverse the string "Python".
Which statement produces "nohtyP"?

feedback.right: The slice [::-1] steps through the string backwards and returns a new string.
feedback.wrong: Use name[::-1]. Strings have no reverse() or sort() method, and reversed() returns an iterator, not a string.

questions.text:
A CSV file contains thousands of records. The developer wants to process one row at a time without loading the entire file into memory.
Which approach is recommended?

feedback.right: csv.reader reads the file lazily, one row at a time, so memory stays flat.
feedback.wrong: Use csv.reader(file), which yields one row at a time. read(), readlines() and list(file) all load the whole file into memory first.

questions.text:
A package contains several modules. The developer wants to make the folder recognizable as a package in older Python versions.
Which file should be included?

feedback.right: An __init__.py file marks a folder as a regular package. It's optional since Python 3.3 but still standard practice.
feedback.wrong: The file is __init__.py. Older Python versions only treat a folder as a package if it has one; setup.py is for packaging and distribution.

questions.text:
A module contains reusable utility functions. Multiple projects need those functions.
What is the primary benefit of placing them in a separate module?

feedback.right: One shared module means you write and fix the code once, and every project picks up the change.
feedback.wrong: The benefit is reuse and easier maintenance: one copy of the code to fix and test. Moving code into a module doesn't make it faster or use less memory.

questions.text:
Why is the following code considered a best practice?
```
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```
options: It ensures the main code runs only when the file is executed directly.

feedback.right: It keeps main() from running when the file is imported, so the module can be reused safely.
feedback.wrong: The guard makes main() run only when the file is executed directly, not on import. It has no effect on speed or syntax errors.

questions.text:
A program receives text with random capitalization.
PYTHON programming
The developer wants the output:
Python Programming
Which method should be used?

feedback.right: title() capitalises the first letter of every word and lowercases the rest.
feedback.wrong: Use title(), which gives Python Programming. capitalize() only capitalises the first word (Python programming), and upper() makes everything uppercase.

questions.text: In a for ... else loop, when does the else block run?
options: After every single iteration of the loop
Only when the loop finishes without hitting break
Only when the loop body raises an exception
Only when the loop runs zero times

feedback.right: The else on a loop runs only if the loop wasn't stopped by break, which makes it handy for 'not found' cases.
feedback.wrong: A loop's else runs only when the loop finishes without a break. It also runs when the loop has zero iterations, but that isn't the only case.

feedback.right: Dog overrides sound(), so a returns Animal and b returns Bark.
feedback.wrong: It prints Animal Bark. Each object uses its own class's method: Animal's for a, Dog's override for b.

questions.text: You must check whether each of 1,00,000 incoming IDs already exists among 50,000 stored IDs. Fastest container for the stored IDs?

feedback.right: A set lookup is O(1) on average, so 100,000 checks stay fast.
feedback.wrong: Use a set. Each list or tuple lookup scans up to 50,000 items; a sorted list needs a binary search (O(log n)), while a set is O(1) on average.

questions.text: Which statement correctly converts a Python dictionary into a JSON string?

feedback.right: json.dumps returns a string; the s stands for string.
feedback.wrong: Use json.dumps(data). json.dump writes to a file object, and load/loads go the other way, from JSON back to Python.

questions.text: Which string method removes leading and trailing whitespace?

feedback.right: strip() removes whitespace from both ends; lstrip() and rstrip() do one side each.
feedback.wrong: Python uses strip(). trim() is the JavaScript name, and remove() and clean() aren't string methods.

questions.text: Which statement correctly creates a dictionary with employee IDs as keys and names as values?

feedback.right: Curly braces with key: value pairs create a dictionary.
feedback.wrong: Dictionaries use curly braces: {101: "John", 102: "Mary"}. Square brackets and parentheses with colons are syntax errors.

questions.text: Which of the following is used to add a new element to the end of a Python list?

feedback.right: append() adds a single item to the end of a list.
feedback.wrong: Use append(). insert() needs a position, extend() adds every item from another iterable, and add() is for sets.

questions.text: Which statement about Python sets is TRUE?
options: Sets maintain insertion order and allow duplicates.

feedback.right: A set keeps only one copy of each value, so duplicates disappear automatically.
feedback.wrong: Sets automatically drop duplicates. They aren't indexable, they don't keep insertion order, and they can hold any hashable type.

questions.text: Which of the following is a valid Python variable name?

feedback.right: Names can contain letters, digits and underscores, but can't start with a digit or be a keyword.
feedback.wrong: user_name is valid. 2user starts with a digit, user-name contains a minus sign, and class is a reserved keyword.

questions.text:

```
print(10 // 3)
```

feedback.right: // is floor division, so 10 // 3 drops the remainder and gives 3.
feedback.wrong: // is floor division: 10 // 3 is 3. 3.33 would come from /, and 1 is the remainder you'd get from %.

questions.text: Which file mode allows reading and writing without deleting existing file content?

feedback.right: r+ opens an existing file for reading and writing without truncating it.
feedback.wrong: Use r+. w and w+ empty the file as soon as it opens, and a only lets you write at the end.

questions.explain: FastAPI automatically serializes dictionaries into JSON.

feedback.right: FastAPI serialises the returned dict to JSON and sets the Content-Type header for you.
feedback.wrong: The client gets JSON. FastAPI converts the returned dict into a JSON response; clients never receive Python objects directly.

questions.explain: File reading is asynchronous.

feedback.right: readFile is asynchronous, so console.log('Done') runs first and the callback fires later.
feedback.wrong: Done prints first. readFile doesn't block; its callback runs once the file has been read, after the synchronous code has finished.

questions.text: A web application makes several API calls one after another, even though they are independent. Which approach improves performance?
options: Execute independent requests concurrently using Promise.all()
questions.explain: Concurrent execution reduces overall waiting time.

feedback.right: Promise.all starts all the requests at once, so the total wait is about as long as the slowest call.
feedback.wrong: Run them concurrently with Promise.all(). Independent calls don't need to wait for each other, so total time drops to roughly the slowest single call.

questions.explain: Async functions return Promises automatically.

feedback.right: An async function wraps its return value in a Promise, and then() receives the resolved 100.
feedback.wrong: It prints 100. test() returns a Promise that resolves to 100, and then(console.log) logs that resolved value.

feedback.wrong: It prints 20. The inner let x shadows the outer one inside the function, so the outer 10 isn't used there.

questions.text: Which practice best improves maintainability in large Python applications?
options: Writing all logic in a single script
Organizing code into reusable modules and packages
questions.explain: Modular code is easier to maintain and test.

feedback.right: Small modules and packages keep related code together, which makes it easier to test, reuse and change.
feedback.wrong: Organise code into reusable modules and packages. A single script, heavy use of globals and copy-pasted functions all make large codebases harder to maintain.

questions.text: What is the primary purpose of a JavaScript Promise?
options: Represent the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation
questions.explain: Promises manage asynchronous workflows.

feedback.right: A Promise is a placeholder for a result that will arrive later, or an error if the work fails.
feedback.wrong: A Promise represents the eventual success or failure of an async operation. It doesn't store state, create classes or parse JSON.

questions.text: Which statement best describes FastAPI?
options: A modern Python framework for building high-performance APIs
questions.explain: FastAPI simplifies API development.

feedback.right: FastAPI is a Python web framework for APIs, built on type hints, Pydantic and async support.
feedback.wrong: FastAPI is a modern Python framework for building fast APIs. It isn't a frontend framework, a database or a testing library.

questions.text: Which JavaScript feature allows a function to continue execution after an asynchronous operation completes without blocking the main thread?
questions.explain: async/await simplifies asynchronous programming.

feedback.right: await pauses only that function until the promise settles, while the main thread keeps running other work.
feedback.wrong: async/await lets a function wait for an async result without blocking the main thread. setInterval just runs code on a timer.

questions.text:
What is the output of the following JavaScript code?

```
console.log(typeof []);
```
questions.explain: Arrays are objects in JavaScript.

feedback.right: Arrays are objects in JavaScript, so typeof returns "object". Use Array.isArray() to check for an array.
feedback.wrong: typeof [] is "object" because arrays are a kind of object. JavaScript has no "array" or "list" type for typeof; use Array.isArray() instead.

questions.text: During API testing, multiple endpoints depend on authentication tokens. What is the best testing approach?
options: Automate token generation and reuse during test execution
questions.explain: Automated authentication improves reliability.

feedback.right: Generating tokens in a setup step keeps tests realistic and stops expired or leaked hard-coded tokens from breaking them.
feedback.wrong: Automate token generation and reuse the token across tests. Hard-coded tokens expire and leak, and skipping authentication leaves the most important paths untested.

questions.text: During API testing, which aspect should be verified in addition to the response body?
options: HTTP status code, headers, and response time
questions.explain: API testing verifies functional and non-functional behavior.

feedback.right: A correct body with the wrong status code or headers is still a bug, and response time tells you about performance.
feedback.wrong: Check the status code, headers and response time as well as the body. Things like screen resolution or CPU temperature have nothing to do with an API's behaviour.

questions.text: Which HTTP method is most appropriate for creating a new resource in a REST API?
questions.explain: POST creates new resources.

feedback.right: POST creates a new resource; the server usually replies 201 Created.
feedback.wrong: Use POST to create resources. GET reads, DELETE removes, and PATCH partly updates something that already exists.

questions.text: What is the primary role of the Node.js Event Loop?
options: Manage asynchronous operations without blocking execution
questions.explain: The Event Loop enables non-blocking I/O.

feedback.right: The event loop runs callbacks when I/O finishes, so one thread can serve many requests without waiting.
feedback.wrong: The event loop handles asynchronous work without blocking. It runs callbacks as I/O completes; it doesn't compile code or store data.

questions.text: A production API built with FastAPI serves thousands of concurrent users. Which combination of practices best improves scalability and maintainability?
options: Place all logic inside route functions and disable validation
Use modular architecture, dependency injection, request validation, proper logging, and automated API testing
Store business logic inside frontend code
Replace REST APIs with print statements
questions.explain: Production APIs require clean architecture and testing.

feedback.right: Modular code, dependency injection, validation, logging and automated tests together keep a big API scalable and easy to change.
feedback.wrong: The answer is the combination: modular architecture, dependency injection, request validation, logging and automated tests. Turning off validation or moving logic to the frontend makes things worse.

options: FastAPI returns a validation error because abc is not an integer
questions.explain: FastAPI validates path parameters using type hints.

feedback.right: The type hint id: int makes FastAPI validate the path, so abc gets a 422 validation error before your code runs.
feedback.wrong: FastAPI returns a 422 validation error. The int type hint is enforced on the path parameter, so abc is rejected before the function runs. Nothing crashes.

questions.text: In a Python project, what is the primary purpose of an __init__.py file inside a directory?
options: Marks the directory as a Python package and enables imports
questions.explain: Packages organize reusable code.

feedback.right: __init__.py marks a directory as a package so its modules can be imported, and it can run package setup code.
feedback.wrong: __init__.py marks the folder as a Python package so imports work. It doesn't store env variables, start the app or compile anything.

questions.text: Which JavaScript keyword declares a block-scoped variable that can be reassigned?
questions.explain: let is block scoped and mutable.

feedback.right: let is block-scoped and can be reassigned. const is block-scoped but can't be reassigned.
feedback.wrong: It's let. var is function-scoped, not block-scoped, and const can't be reassigned.

questions.text: A Node.js API becomes slow because CPU-intensive calculations are performed directly inside request handlers. What is the best architectural improvement?
options: Move CPU-intensive tasks to worker threads or background processing

feedback.right: Node runs JavaScript on one thread, so heavy CPU work blocks every request. Worker threads or a job queue take it off that thread.
feedback.wrong: Move CPU-heavy work to worker threads or a background job. A longer timeout only hides the problem, because the blocked event loop still stalls every request.

questions.text: FastAPI automatically generates API documentation using:
questions.explain: Automatic documentation improves API usability.

feedback.right: FastAPI builds an OpenAPI schema from your routes and serves Swagger UI at /docs.
feedback.wrong: FastAPI uses OpenAPI and Swagger UI (at /docs). TensorFlow, Docker Compose and Flask templates have nothing to do with API docs.

questions.text: Which built-in Node.js module is commonly used for reading and writing files?
questions.explain: The fs module provides file system operations.

feedback.right: fs is Node's file system module: readFile, writeFile, streams and so on.
feedback.wrong: Use the fs module for files. http serves web requests, path handles file paths, and events provides event emitters.

questions.text: A FastAPI endpoint accepts user input. What is the best way to validate incoming data?
questions.explain: Pydantic performs automatic validation.

feedback.right: Pydantic models validate types and required fields automatically and return clear errors.
feedback.wrong: Use Pydantic models. FastAPI validates the request body against them and returns 422 with details. Manual string checks are fragile, and frontend validation can be bypassed.

questions.text: A client receives HTTP status code 404. What does it indicate?
questions.explain: Status codes communicate API outcomes.

feedback.right: 404 means the server couldn't find the requested resource.
feedback.wrong: 404 means Not Found. 401 is unauthorised, 500 is an internal server error and 200 is success.

questions.text: A FastAPI application contains business logic directly inside every route. Which architectural improvement is most appropriate?
options: Move business logic into a separate service layer
Increase the number of API routes
Merge all APIs into one endpoint
questions.explain: Separation of concerns improves maintainability.

feedback.right: A service layer keeps routes thin and puts business logic somewhere you can reuse and unit-test.
feedback.wrong: Move business logic into a service layer. Routes should just handle HTTP; more routes or less validation don't fix the coupling.

questions.text: A production Python script unexpectedly fails. Which practice makes diagnosing the issue easiest?
options: Structured logging with meaningful log levels
questions.explain: Logging helps identify failures efficiently.

feedback.right: Structured logs with levels let you filter for errors and trace exactly what happened before the failure.
feedback.wrong: Use structured logging with sensible levels. Print statements have no levels or timestamps, and removing exception handling hides the cause.

questions.text: A FastAPI service runs with four worker processes. A developer stores a login session dictionary in a module-level variable. A user logs in successfully, but the next request sometimes reports the session as missing. What change directly addresses the architectural problem?
options: Make the dictionary global with a different variable name
Store shared session state in an external shared store such as Redis or a database

feedback.right: Each worker process has its own memory, so a module-level dict isn't shared. Redis or a database gives all workers the same session data.
feedback.wrong: Store sessions in a shared store like Redis or a database. Each of the four workers has its own memory, so a session saved in one isn't visible to the others.

questions.text: A service uses JWT authentication. A valid token is presented, but the token's `aud` claim does not match the API's expected audience. What should the API do?
options: Treat it as an anonymous request
Reject the token because its intended audience is not the API
Accept it because the signature is valid

feedback.right: The aud claim says who the token is for. A token meant for another service must be rejected even if its signature is valid.
feedback.wrong: Reject it. A valid signature only proves who issued the token; a wrong aud means it was issued for a different API.

questions.text:
Consider the following FastAPI route:

```
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()

class User(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: int

@app.post("/users")
def create_user(user: User):
    if user.age < 18:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=400,
            detail="Minor"
        )
    return user
```

A valid JSON request is sent with:
```
{
    "name": "Arun",
    "age": 16
}
```

What happens when the request is processed?
options: FastAPI returns 422 Unprocessable Entity because age is below 18.
The API returns 200 OK with the user details.
The function raises an HTTPException with status code 400 and detail "Minor".
Pydantic automatically changes the age to 18.

feedback.right: The body passes Pydantic validation, since 16 is a valid int, so your own check runs and raises 400 Minor.
feedback.wrong: The function raises HTTPException 400 with detail Minor. Pydantic only checks that age is an int, which 16 is; the under-18 rule is your own code, not a 422.

questions.text: A test for a FastAPI endpoint modifies shared database state, causing later tests to fail depending on execution order. Which testing strategy addresses the root cause?
options: Use isolated fixtures with rollback or cleanup so each test has controlled database state
Run tests only in one fixed order

feedback.right: Isolated fixtures (a transaction that rolls back, or cleanup) give every test a known starting state, so order no longer matters.
feedback.wrong: Give each test isolated state with fixtures that roll back or clean up. A fixed run order only hides the coupling, and production data makes it worse.

questions.text: A file-upload endpoint accepts a 500 MB file, but the application business limit is 10 MB. The current code fully processes the upload and checks size afterward. What is the strongest correction?
options: Process all 500 MB and reject it afterward
Enforce upload/body limits before expensive processing and validate content during ingestion
Compress the file repeatedly in memory

feedback.right: Reject oversized uploads at the body-size limit so the server never spends time and memory on 500 MB it will refuse.
feedback.wrong: Enforce size limits before processing and validate while reading the upload. Processing 500 MB first wastes resources and opens the door to denial of service.

questions.text: An API returns HTTP 204 after successfully deleting a resource. Which response-body behavior is correct?
options: The response must contain JSON error details
The response contains no message body
The response must use status 201 instead
The response must contain the deleted object

feedback.right: 204 No Content means success with an empty body.
feedback.wrong: A 204 response has no body. That's what No Content means; returning the deleted object would need 200.

questions.text:
Consider the following code
```
import asyncio

async def task(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    return n * 2

async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(task(2), task(3))
    print(results)

asyncio.run(main())
```
What is the value of results?

feedback.right: gather runs both tasks and returns their results in order as a list: [4, 6].
feedback.wrong: results is [4, 6]. gather returns a list of each task's return value, in the order you passed them, and each task doubles its input.

questions.text: A Node.js route calls an async database function. The promise rejects, but the error is not propagated to centralized error middleware. What should be ensured?
options: The response should always be HTTP 200
The rejected promise must be caught or propagated to the framework's centralized error handler
The database should send the error directly to the browser

feedback.right: Unhandled rejections skip Express's error middleware. Catch them and call next(err), or use a wrapper that does it for you.
feedback.wrong: The rejection must be caught or passed on (for example next(err) in Express) so the central error handler sees it. Ignoring it can crash the process or leave the request hanging.

questions.text: A FastAPI endpoint performs three independent external API calls, each taking about 500 ms. The endpoint is currently synchronous and performs them sequentially. The calls have no data dependency. Which implementation most directly reduces the endpoint's I/O waiting time?
options: Convert the calls into database joins
Use an async route with an async HTTP client and await the three independent calls concurrently

feedback.right: With an async client and asyncio.gather, the three 500 ms calls overlap, so the endpoint waits about 500 ms instead of 1.5 s.
feedback.wrong: Make the route async and await the three calls concurrently with an async HTTP client. They're independent, so the total wait drops from about 1.5 s to about 500 ms.

questions.text: A FastAPI application has a reusable dependency that opens a database session and yields it to the endpoint. The session must close even when the endpoint raises an exception. Which implementation pattern is appropriate?
options: Close the session before yielding it
Open the session at import time and never close it
Use a generator dependency with cleanup after `yield`
Create the session after the endpoint returns

feedback.right: A yield dependency hands the session to the endpoint, and the code after yield (in a finally block) always closes it.
feedback.wrong: Use a generator dependency: yield the session and close it after the yield, ideally in a finally block. FastAPI runs that cleanup even when the endpoint raises.

questions.text: Two clients simultaneously attempt to create a customer with the same unique email. Both application processes check for existence before insertion. What guarantees uniqueness under the race condition?
options: A Python dictionary check in each process
A database UNIQUE constraint enforced during insertion

feedback.right: Only the database sees every insert, so a UNIQUE constraint is the one check both processes can't slip past.
feedback.wrong: Use a UNIQUE constraint in the database. Two processes can both pass a check-then-insert at the same moment; the constraint rejects the second insert.

questions.text: A FastAPI API is deployed behind a reverse proxy. Generated HTTPS links incorrectly use `http://` because the application sees the proxy-to-app connection instead of the original scheme. Which configuration area should be corrected?
options: Trusted proxy forwarding headers and application proxy configuration

feedback.right: The proxy ends HTTPS and forwards plain HTTP. Trusting its X-Forwarded-Proto header tells the app the original scheme.
feedback.wrong: Fix the proxy header settings: trust X-Forwarded-Proto and similar headers (e.g. Uvicorn's --proxy-headers). The app only sees the plain HTTP hop from the proxy.

questions.text: A Node.js service receives a 2 GB CSV file. Loading the complete file into memory causes process crashes. Which implementation is most appropriate?
options: Increase the JavaScript variable name length
Duplicate the file into memory before parsing
Convert the entire CSV into one large string
Use streaming/backpressure-aware processing with bounded memory

feedback.right: Streaming reads the file in chunks, and backpressure stops the reader from outrunning the processing, so memory stays bounded.
feedback.wrong: Stream the file with backpressure, for example with a streaming CSV parser. Loading 2 GB into memory, or copying it, is what causes the crash.

questions.text: A FastAPI endpoint accepts an `order_id` path parameter typed as `int`. A client sends `/orders/abc`. The endpoint contains database logic that would otherwise raise a custom error. What occurs first?
options: The database query executes and receives `abc`
FastAPI request validation rejects the path parameter before endpoint business logic executes

feedback.right: FastAPI validates the int path parameter before calling your function, so abc gets a 422 and the database code never runs.
feedback.wrong: Validation happens first: abc isn't an int, so FastAPI returns 422 before the endpoint runs. The database query never receives abc.

questions.text:
Consider this Python code in a package: # pkg/utils.py
```
x = 10
def update():
     global x
     x += 5
# main.py
from pkg.utils  import x, update
update()
print(x)
```
What is printed?

feedback.right: from ... import x copies the current value into main's own name. update() changes utils.x, but main's x stays 10.
feedback.wrong: It prints 10. The import binds main's own x to 10. update() rebinds pkg.utils.x to 15, but main's name still points to the old value.

questions.text: A Node.js application starts three independent database queries sequentially with `await`, even though no query depends on another. Which change reduces avoidable waiting time?
options: Add a fixed delay between queries
Convert query results to HTML before awaiting
Start the independent promises together and await them collectively

feedback.right: Start all three queries first, then await Promise.all, so the waiting overlaps instead of adding up.
feedback.wrong: Start the independent queries together and await them with Promise.all. Awaiting one at a time makes the total wait the sum of all three.

questions.text: A developer builds SQL using `f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE id={user_id}"`, where user_id comes from the request. Which correction provides the strongest primary defense?
options: Hide the SQL statement from the client

feedback.right: Parameterised queries send the value separately from the SQL text, so input can never change the query's structure.
feedback.wrong: Use parameterised queries (prepared statements). Base64-encoding or hiding the SQL doesn't stop injection; only keeping data out of the SQL text does.

questions.text: A REST API receives `GET /products?page=1&page_size=100000`. The database can technically return the data, but the service must protect itself from excessive responses. Which API-level control is most appropriate?
options: Allow the request because GET is read-only
Validate page_size and enforce a server-side maximum
Return all rows and let the browser truncate them

feedback.right: A server-side cap on page_size stops a single request from pulling huge result sets and overloading the service.
feedback.wrong: Validate page_size and enforce a maximum on the server. GET being read-only doesn't make a 100,000-row response cheap, and the client can't be trusted to limit it.

feedback.right: The arrow function closes over the inner x. x++ returns the old value and then increments, so you get 20, then 21.
feedback.wrong: It prints 20 then 21. The closure keeps the inner x (20), and x++ returns the value before incrementing it.

questions.text: A production application must avoid exposing stack traces but still retain complete diagnostic information for engineers. Which design is best?
options: Log detailed exceptions server-side while returning a generic error response with a correlation ID to clients
Return the full stack trace to every client

feedback.right: Detailed logs stay on the server, and the correlation ID lets engineers match a user's generic error to the exact log entry.
feedback.wrong: Log full details on the server and return a generic error with a correlation ID. Stack traces leak internals to attackers, and suppressing logs leaves engineers blind.

questions.text: A REST endpoint supports `PUT /users/42` and is designed to replace the complete user representation. The same valid PUT request may be sent repeatedly. Which property should the endpoint have?
options: Mandatory creation of a second resource

feedback.right: PUT replaces the whole resource, so sending the same request again leaves the same final state. That's idempotency.
feedback.wrong: PUT should be idempotent: repeating the same request gives the same result as sending it once. That makes retries safe.

questions.text: A FastAPI response model contains `id`, `email`, and `name`, while the internal ORM object also contains `password_hash`. What is the key security advantage of returning through the response model?
options: It deletes password_hash from the database
It constrains the serialized public response schema and prevents accidental exposure of internal fields

feedback.right: The response model acts as an allow-list, so only id, email and name are serialised and password_hash never leaves the server.
feedback.wrong: The response model limits what gets serialised, so internal fields like password_hash are never sent. It doesn't delete or encrypt anything in the database.

questions.text: A service must prevent an authenticated user from accessing `/customers/900` when the customer belongs to another tenant. Authentication succeeds, but authorization must be tenant-aware. Where should this check be enforced?
options: Only by hiding the customer ID
In backend authorization/business logic using the authenticated tenant identity and resource ownership

feedback.right: Only the backend can be trusted. It must check that the resource belongs to the caller's tenant on every request.
feedback.wrong: Enforce it in backend authorisation logic, comparing the user's tenant with the resource's owner. Frontend checks and hidden IDs are easy to bypass.

questions.text: A JavaScript frontend executes `fetch()` and expects HTTP 500 to enter the promise `catch` block automatically. The code does not check `response.ok`. What is the technical issue?
options: JSON parsing automatically retries the request
fetch resolves normally for HTTP error statuses; application code must inspect the response status
HTTP 500 is converted to HTTP 200 by the browser

feedback.right: fetch only rejects on network failures. A 500 is a normal response, so you have to check response.ok yourself.
feedback.wrong: fetch resolves for any HTTP status, including 500. It only rejects on network errors, so check response.ok or response.status and throw yourself.

questions.text: A Python service catches a low-level database exception and raises a domain-specific `PaymentPersistenceError`. The developer wants the original exception to remain available in the traceback. Which syntax is appropriate?
options: Raise the domain exception using `raise PaymentPersistenceError(...) from exc`
Convert the exception to a string and discard it

feedback.right: raise ... from exc chains the original exception, so the traceback shows both the domain error and its cause.
feedback.wrong: Use raise PaymentPersistenceError(...) from exc. That chains the original exception as __cause__, so it still shows in the traceback.

questions.text: Which Azure Storage service is most suitable for storing images, videos, and documents?
questions.explain: Blob Storage is optimized for unstructured data.

feedback.right: Blob Storage is built for unstructured files like images, videos and documents.
feedback.wrong: Use Azure Blob Storage for files like images and videos. Queue Storage holds messages, Table Storage holds key-value entities, and DNS resolves names.

questions.text: Azure SQL Database is an example of which cloud service model?
questions.explain: Azure SQL is a managed database service.

feedback.right: Azure manages the server, OS and database engine; you just use the database. That's PaaS.
feedback.wrong: Azure SQL Database is PaaS: Microsoft runs the servers, patching and backups, and you manage only your data and schema. Running SQL Server on a VM would be IaaS.

questions.text: An application deployed to Azure App Service cannot connect to the database because the connection string differs between development and production. What is the recommended solution?
options: Configure the connection string as an App Service environment variable
Store the connection string inside the application source code
questions.explain: Configuration should be externalized.

feedback.right: App Service settings let each environment supply its own connection string without changing the code.
feedback.wrong: Put the connection string in App Service configuration as an environment variable. Hard-coding it in source breaks other environments and leaks secrets into the repo.

questions.text: During deployment to Azure App Service, environment variables are primarily used to:
options: Store configuration values such as API keys and database connection strings
questions.explain: Configuration should be separated from code.

feedback.right: Environment variables keep configuration like keys and connection strings out of the code, so each environment can differ.
feedback.wrong: They store configuration such as API keys and connection strings, separate from the code. They don't hold images or affect CPU speed.

questions.text: In Microsoft Azure, which hierarchy correctly represents how resources are organized?
questions.explain: Azure follows a hierarchical resource organization.

feedback.right: A subscription contains resource groups, and each resource group contains resources.
feedback.wrong: The order is Subscription, then Resource Group, then Resource. Subscriptions hold resource groups, and resource groups hold the actual resources.

questions.text: What is the primary purpose of an Azure Subscription?
options: To provide a billing, access control, and resource management boundary
questions.explain: Subscriptions manage billing and resources.

feedback.right: A subscription is the boundary for billing, access control and quotas.
feedback.wrong: A subscription is a billing, access control and management boundary. It can hold every kind of resource, not just VMs or storage.

questions.text: An Azure Region is best described as:
options: A geographical area containing one or more Azure datacenters
questions.explain: Regions host Azure services.

feedback.right: A region is a geographic area with one or more datacenters, such as East US or Central India.
feedback.wrong: A region is a geographic area containing one or more Azure datacenters. It isn't a single VM, storage account or billing unit.

questions.text: Which statement about Azure Resource Groups is correct?
options: Resources from multiple subscriptions can exist in a single Resource Group
Every resource belongs to exactly one Resource Group
A Resource Group cannot be deleted
Resource Groups automatically create virtual machines
questions.explain: Every Azure resource belongs to one Resource Group.

feedback.right: Every Azure resource lives in exactly one resource group, though you can move it to another.
feedback.wrong: Every resource belongs to exactly one resource group. A group can't span subscriptions, can be deleted, and never creates resources on its own.

questions.text: GitHub Actions are primarily used to:
options: Automate build, testing, and deployment workflows
questions.explain: GitHub Actions support CI/CD.

feedback.right: GitHub Actions runs workflows on events such as a push, typically to build, test and deploy code (CI/CD).
feedback.wrong: GitHub Actions automates build, test and deployment workflows. It doesn't create subscriptions, store logs or configure networks.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of Software as a Service (SaaS)?
questions.explain: SaaS delivers complete software to users.

feedback.right: Microsoft 365 is finished software you just sign in and use, which is what SaaS means.
feedback.wrong: Microsoft 365 is SaaS: complete software delivered over the internet. VMs are IaaS, and App Service and AKS are platform services you deploy your own code to.

questions.text: An Azure Storage Account can contain:
options: Blob containers, File Shares, Queues, and Tables
questions.explain: Storage Accounts support multiple storage services.

feedback.right: One storage account can hold four services: blobs, file shares, queues and tables.
feedback.wrong: A storage account can contain blob containers, file shares, queues and tables. VMs, SQL databases and App Services are separate resources.

questions.text: A developer wants to deploy a Python FastAPI application without configuring an operating system. Which Azure service is most appropriate?
questions.explain: App Service simplifies deployments.

feedback.right: App Service runs your code on a managed platform, so there's no OS to install or patch.
feedback.wrong: Use Azure App Service. A VM would make you manage the operating system yourself, and Blob Storage and Backup don't run applications.

questions.text: Which cloud service model does Azure Virtual Machine belong to?

feedback.right: A VM gives you raw compute: you manage the OS and everything on it. That's IaaS.
feedback.wrong: Azure VMs are IaaS. Azure supplies the virtual hardware, and you manage the OS, patches and software.

questions.text: A company wants Microsoft to manage the operating system while developers only deploy application code. Which Azure service best meets this requirement?
questions.explain: App Service abstracts infrastructure.

feedback.right: App Service is PaaS: Microsoft runs and patches the OS, and you only deploy code.
feedback.wrong: Use Azure App Service. With a VM you manage the OS yourself, and VNets and storage accounts don't run code.

questions.text: Which Azure service allows developers to deploy web applications without managing the underlying operating system?
questions.explain: App Service is a Platform as a Service offering.

feedback.right: App Service hosts web apps on a managed platform, so the OS is not your concern.
feedback.wrong: It's Azure App Service. VMs make you manage the OS, and AKS still leaves you managing clusters and containers.

questions.text: Why are Resource Groups used in Azure?
options: To logically group related Azure resources for management and lifecycle operations
questions.explain: Resource Groups simplify management.

feedback.right: Resource groups bundle related resources so you can manage access, cost and deletion together.
feedback.wrong: Resource groups logically group related resources so you can manage, secure and delete them together. They sit inside subscriptions, not in place of them.

questions.text: Which Azure service is primarily used to create and manage virtual machines?
questions.explain: Azure VM provides Infrastructure as a Service.

feedback.right: Azure Virtual Machines is the IaaS service for creating and running VMs.
feedback.wrong: Use Azure Virtual Machines. App Service hosts web apps, SQL Database is a managed database, and Blob Storage holds files.

questions.text: Which deployment model allows an organization to use both on-premises infrastructure and public cloud together?
questions.explain: Hybrid Cloud combines environments.

feedback.right: Hybrid cloud connects on-premises infrastructure with public cloud so they work as one environment.
feedback.wrong: That's hybrid cloud: on-premises and public cloud used together. Private cloud is just your own infrastructure, and public cloud is just the provider's.

questions.text: Which Azure feature allows applications to securely store sensitive values like API keys and secrets?
questions.explain: Key Vault securely stores secrets.

feedback.right: Key Vault stores secrets, keys and certificates with access control and audit logs.
feedback.wrong: Use Azure Key Vault for secrets. Monitor watches metrics and logs, Backup protects data, and plain Storage isn't designed for secrets.

questions.text: A team has developed a FastAPI application, stores code in GitHub, deploys to Azure App Service using GitHub Actions, and keeps secrets in environment variables. Which statement best describes this workflow?
options: Manual deployment using Infrastructure as a Service
Automated CI/CD deployment following cloud application deployment best practices
questions.explain: CI/CD automates application deployment.

feedback.right: Code goes from GitHub to App Service automatically through Actions, with secrets kept out of the code. That's CI/CD done right.
feedback.wrong: This is automated CI/CD following cloud deployment best practices. Nothing here is manual, IaaS-based or on-premises.

questions.text: What is the primary purpose of Azure Availability Zones?
options: To improve application availability by distributing resources across separate physical locations within a region
questions.explain: Availability Zones improve fault tolerance.

feedback.right: Zones are physically separate datacenters in one region, so spreading across them survives a single site failure.
feedback.wrong: Availability Zones raise availability by placing resources in separate physical locations within a region. They don't change cost, memory or subscription layout.

questions.text: A production web application must continue running even if one datacenter within an Azure Region fails. Which Azure feature best supports this requirement?
questions.explain: Availability Zones improve resilience.

feedback.right: Running instances in more than one zone keeps the app up if one datacenter in the region fails.
feedback.wrong: Use Availability Zones. Each zone is a separate datacenter, so instances in other zones keep running. Resource groups and Monitor don't add redundancy.

questions.text: A startup needs a server that gives full control over the operating system. Which Azure service should they choose?
questions.explain: VMs provide full OS control.

feedback.right: A VM gives full control of the OS: install anything, change settings, apply your own patches.
feedback.wrong: Choose an Azure Virtual Machine. App Service, SQL Database and Functions are managed services that hide the OS from you.

questions.text: Which Azure Storage service is commonly used to create shared network file storage?
questions.explain: Azure Files provides managed file shares.

feedback.right: Azure Files provides SMB/NFS file shares that many machines can mount at once.
feedback.wrong: Use Azure Files for shared network drives. Blob Storage is object storage over HTTP, not a mountable file share.

questions.text: Before GitHub Actions can deploy to Azure App Service, which step is commonly required?
options: Configure deployment credentials or publish profile as GitHub Secrets
questions.explain: Secure authentication is required.

feedback.right: The workflow needs credentials (a publish profile or service principal) stored as GitHub Secrets to deploy.
feedback.wrong: GitHub Actions needs deployment credentials, such as a publish profile, saved as GitHub Secrets. Blob accounts or bigger VMs aren't part of it.

questions.text: A team wants to deploy application code without managing the operating system, patching, or runtime infrastructure. Which service model best matches the requirement?

feedback.right: PaaS handles the OS, patching and runtime, so you only deploy code.
feedback.wrong: That's PaaS. With IaaS you still manage the OS and patching, and bare metal or colocation means managing even more.

questions.text: A company wants separate billing, quotas, and administrative boundaries for business units. Which Azure construct is most relevant?

feedback.right: Subscriptions give each business unit its own billing, quotas and admin boundary.
feedback.wrong: Use subscriptions. They're the boundary for billing, quotas and administration. Availability zones are about resilience, not ownership.

questions.text: A workload needs an identity that can access a specific Azure resource without storing a long-lived credential in application configuration. Which capability is most appropriate?

feedback.right: A managed identity gets credentials from Azure automatically, so there's no secret in your config to rotate or leak.
feedback.wrong: Use a managed identity. Azure handles the credential for you, while a shared admin account or stored secret is exactly what you want to avoid.

questions.text: A bank keeps regulated databases in its datacenter but uses Azure for scalable application processing during peak periods. Which deployment model best describes this architecture?

feedback.right: Regulated data stays on-premises and Azure handles burst capacity, which makes it a hybrid cloud.
feedback.wrong: It's hybrid cloud: an on-premises datacenter and Azure working together. Neither public-only nor private-only fits.

questions.text: A deployment must create a virtual network, subnet, VM, and storage account consistently across multiple environments. Which approach best prevents configuration drift?
options: Use screenshots of the first environment
Create resources manually in the portal each time
Use declarative infrastructure definitions with parameterized deployments

feedback.right: Infrastructure as Code (ARM, Bicep, Terraform) with parameters builds identical environments every time.
feedback.wrong: Use declarative infrastructure as code with parameters, such as Bicep or Terraform. Manual portal work is exactly what causes configuration drift.

questions.text: A pipeline should automatically deploy after code is merged but require explicit approval before production. Which workflow best matches?
options: Build and test automatically, then require an approval gate before production deployment

feedback.right: Build and tests run automatically, and a manual approval gate guards production.
feedback.wrong: Build and test automatically, then add an approval gate before production. Approving after the deploy or deploying before tests defeats the point.

questions.text: A developer can view production resources but must not modify or delete them. Which access model best satisfies this requirement?
options: Assign a read-only RBAC role at the appropriate scope

feedback.right: A read-only role (Reader) at the right scope lets them view resources but not change them.
feedback.wrong: Assign a read-only RBAC role such as Reader at the right scope. Owner allows changes, and sharing admin credentials breaks accountability.

questions.text: A company wants separate permissions and lifecycle management for development and production resources while keeping them under one Azure subscription. Which structure is most appropriate?
options: Use separate resource groups with scoped RBAC assignments
Give all developers subscription Owner access

feedback.right: Separate resource groups with RBAC scoped to each give dev and prod their own permissions and lifecycle.
feedback.wrong: Use separate resource groups with RBAC scoped to each one. Giving everyone subscription Owner removes any separation between dev and prod.

questions.text:
Consider the following deployment:

Azure Region
```
│
├── Availability Zone 1 → Application Instance A
├── Availability Zone 2 → Application Instance B
└── Availability Zone 3 → Application Instance C
```

If one availability zone becomes unavailable, what is the primary benefit of this architecture?
options: The application can continue operating using instances in other zones
All resources are automatically moved to another Azure region

feedback.right: If one zone fails, the instances in the other two zones keep serving traffic.
feedback.wrong: The app keeps running on the instances in the other zones. Azure doesn't move resources to another region automatically.

questions.text: A team wants resources to be grouped by environment and cost center for governance and cost analysis. Which Azure metadata feature is appropriate?

feedback.right: Tags are key-value labels like env=prod or costcenter=42 that you can filter and report costs by.
feedback.wrong: Use resource tags, such as env and costcenter labels, for governance and cost reports. DNS records and zones have nothing to do with grouping.

questions.text: A resource group is deleted accidentally. What lifecycle behavior is important for resources managed within that group?
options: The resources in that resource group are generally deleted with it
The entire Azure tenant is deleted

feedback.right: Deleting a resource group deletes every resource inside it, which is why resource locks exist.
feedback.wrong: The resources in the group are deleted along with it. Use resource locks to prevent accidental deletion. The region and tenant aren't affected.

questions.text: A distributed application needs a simple asynchronous queue so producers can place messages while workers process them later. Which service best fits?

feedback.right: Queue Storage holds messages so producers and workers can run independently and at different speeds.
feedback.wrong: Use Azure Queue Storage for simple message queues. Blob Storage and Files store files, and DNS resolves names.

questions.text: An organization needs a NoSQL key-value data store for simple entities without relational joins. Which Azure service is the closest fit?

feedback.right: Table Storage is a NoSQL key-value store for simple entities, with no joins.
feedback.wrong: Use Azure Table Storage. SQL Database is relational, Files is file shares, and a Load Balancer distributes traffic.

questions.text: A developer needs to read production resources for troubleshooting but must not create, modify, or delete them. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Assign an appropriate read-only RBAC role at the required scope

feedback.right: A read-only role such as Reader, assigned at the needed scope, allows troubleshooting without any write access.
feedback.wrong: Assign a read-only role like Reader at the needed scope. Contributor and Owner can modify and delete resources.

questions.text: A CI/CD pipeline must prevent production deployment when automated tests fail. Where should the test validation occur?

feedback.right: Tests run before the production stage, so a failure stops the pipeline before anything ships.
feedback.wrong: Run tests before the production deployment stage. Testing after deploying means broken code is already live.

questions.text: A company must keep customer data within a legally specified geographic boundary. Which Azure architecture decision is most directly affected?
options: Region selection and data residency requirements

feedback.right: Data residency rules decide which regions you're allowed to store and process data in.
feedback.wrong: Region selection is directly affected. Data residency laws limit where data can be stored, which means choosing regions inside that boundary.

questions.text: A storage workload consists of millions of images accessed as objects over HTTPS. Which Azure storage service is designed for this workload?

feedback.right: Blob Storage is object storage reached over HTTPS, made for millions of images.
feedback.wrong: Use Blob Storage for objects served over HTTPS. Azure Files is mounted as a file share, and Queue Storage holds messages.

questions.text: A cloud application needs redundancy against a regional disaster, not merely a single-zone failure. Which additional architecture should be evaluated?
options: A multi-region architecture or disaster-recovery strategy
Another VM in the same zone only

feedback.right: Zones protect against one datacenter failing. Surviving a whole-region outage needs multi-region deployment or disaster recovery.
feedback.wrong: Look at a multi-region or disaster-recovery setup. Bigger disks or more VMs in the same zone can't survive a whole region going down.

questions.text: A developer needs to manage resources in one production resource group but must not modify resources in another group. What is the strongest RBAC design?
options: Assign Owner at the subscription scope
Assign the required role at the specific production resource-group scope

feedback.right: Scoping the role to that one resource group gives exactly the access needed and nothing else (least privilege).
feedback.wrong: Assign the role at the production resource group's scope. Subscription Owner or Global Administrator would also give access to the other group.

questions.text: A deployment template creates resources with dependencies. One resource must exist before another can be provisioned. Which capability supports this relationship?
options: Declarative resource dependencies/references in the deployment definition

feedback.right: Templates declare dependencies (dependsOn or references), so Azure creates resources in the right order.
feedback.wrong: Use declared dependencies or references in the template, such as dependsOn in ARM. DNS TTL and storage tiers have nothing to do with deployment order.

questions.text: A regulated organization requires a cloud environment dedicated to its own organizational controls and workloads. Which deployment model best matches?

feedback.right: A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation, which suits strict regulatory control.
feedback.wrong: That's a private cloud: infrastructure dedicated to one organisation. Public cloud is shared, and hybrid mixes on-premises with public.

questions.text: An application must tolerate failure of a single Azure datacenter facility while remaining within the same Azure region. Which design is most appropriate?
options: Deploy redundant application instances across availability zones
Store only a local copy of the application
Deploy all instances in one availability zone

feedback.right: Redundant instances in several zones survive the loss of one datacenter without leaving the region.
feedback.wrong: Deploy redundant instances across availability zones. A bigger VM or everything in one zone still fails with that datacenter.

questions.text: A business application requires relational transactions, SQL queries, constraints, and managed database operations. Which Azure service category is appropriate?

feedback.right: Azure SQL Database gives you relational tables, transactions and constraints as a managed service.
feedback.wrong: Use Azure SQL Database for relational data and transactions. Queue and Blob Storage don't support SQL queries or constraints, and CDN caches content.

questions.text: A company needs to audit who created, deleted, or modified Azure resources. Which Azure capability provides resource-level control-plane activity records?

feedback.right: The Activity Log records control-plane operations: who created, changed or deleted which resource, and when.
feedback.wrong: Use the Azure Activity Log. It records who created, modified or deleted resources. The other options don't track control-plane changes.

questions.text: A company wants Azure to provide physical infrastructure while multiple customers use logically isolated resources. Which deployment model is this?

feedback.right: In public cloud the provider owns the hardware and many customers share it, isolated logically.
feedback.wrong: That's public cloud: shared provider-owned infrastructure with logical isolation between customers. Private cloud and single-tenant setups serve one organisation.
