questions.text: An application needs to retrieve secrets from Azure without embedding a client secret in its source code. Which Azure capability is designed for this scenario?
options: Managed identity with Azure Key Vault

feedback.right: The app authenticates with its managed identity and reads secrets from Key Vault, so no client secret lives in the code.
feedback.wrong: Use a managed identity with Key Vault. Azure supplies the identity's credentials, so there's nothing to embed. Public blob access would expose secrets instead.

questions.text: An application deployed in one Azure region has high latency for users on another continent. Which architectural factor should be evaluated first?
options: Geographic placement of compute/data relative to users

feedback.right: Distance adds latency, so the first thing to check is where compute and data sit relative to users. Extra regions or a CDN help.
feedback.wrong: Check where compute and data are placed relative to users. Users on another continent pay for the round-trip distance; tags and names don't affect speed.

questions.text: A team wants infrastructure changes to be reviewable, versioned, and reproducible before deployment. Which practice best supports this?
options: Make all changes manually in the portal
Store declarative infrastructure definitions in version control and deploy them through automation

feedback.right: Infrastructure as Code in Git gets pull-request review, history and repeatable automated deploys.
feedback.wrong: Keep declarative infrastructure definitions in version control and deploy them through a pipeline. Manual portal changes can't be reviewed or reproduced.

questions.text: A storage account contains confidential documents. The security requirement is to prevent anonymous public access. Which control should be applied?
options: Publish the URL in source control
Disable or restrict public access and require authenticated authorization

feedback.right: Turning off anonymous access and requiring authenticated, authorised requests keeps confidential blobs private.
feedback.wrong: Disable or restrict public access and require authentication (Entra ID or SAS). Enabling public container access is the exact opposite of what's needed.

questions.text: A company migrates an existing application to Azure but requires OS-level control because it uses a custom kernel module. Which Azure service model is the most appropriate?

feedback.right: Only IaaS (a VM) gives you control of the OS and kernel, which a custom kernel module needs.
feedback.wrong: It has to be IaaS. A custom kernel module needs OS-level control, which PaaS and SaaS deliberately hide from you.

questions.text: A smaller Linear Regression error generally indicates that:
options: The model uses more attention heads
The predicted continuous values are closer to the actual target values
The model has classified more examples correctly
questions.explain: Regression error measures prediction differences.

feedback.right: Regression error (such as MSE or MAE) measures how far predictions are from the true values, so smaller means closer.
feedback.wrong: Smaller error means the predicted values are closer to the actual targets. Counting correctly classified examples is a classification metric, not regression.

questions.text: A company uses KNN to predict whether a customer will purchase a product. One feature is "annual income" ranging from 20,000 to 1,000,000, while another is "number of website visits" ranging from 1 to 50. The model mostly bases decisions on income. What is the likely cause?
options: The number of neighbors is automatically set too high
The training labels are necessarily incorrect
The large numerical scale of income is dominating distance calculations
questions.explain: KNN is sensitive to feature scales.

feedback.right: KNN uses distances, so a feature measured in hundreds of thousands drowns out one that ranges from 1 to 50. Scale the features first.
feedback.wrong: Income's huge scale dominates the distance calculation. KNN handles numbers fine; standardise or normalise the features so each one counts.

questions.text: A KNN classifier gives excellent accuracy on the training dataset but performs poorly on unseen data when K=1. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The model is performing clustering instead of classification
The classifier is highly sensitive to individual training examples and may be overfitting

feedback.right: With K=1 each prediction copies the single closest training point, noise included, which is classic overfitting.
feedback.wrong: K=1 overfits: it memorises every training point, noise included. Training accuracy is perfect, but it doesn't generalise. Underfitting comes from a very large K.

questions.text: A team compares a Linear Regression model, KNN, and K-Means for predicting the future sales amount of each customer. Which statement correctly identifies the fundamental issue with this comparison?
options: K-Means always gives better numerical predictions than regression
KNN can only be used for clustering
K-Means is unsupervised and does not directly learn a continuous target prediction task, while Linear Regression is designed for such targets
Linear Regression cannot work with numerical targets
questions.explain: The learning objective must match the problem type.

feedback.right: K-Means only groups data. It has no target to predict, so it can't be compared with regression on sales amounts.
feedback.wrong: K-Means is unsupervised and doesn't predict a target value, so it doesn't belong in a sales-prediction comparison. Linear Regression (and KNN regression) can predict numbers.

questions.text: A sentence contains the words "The animal didn't cross the road because it was injured." The model needs to determine what "it" refers to. Which capability of attention is most relevant?
options: Assigning every token the same weight
Giving greater importance to relevant contextual tokens when constructing the representation of "it"
Converting the sentence directly into a numerical target
questions.explain: Attention helps resolve contextual relationships.

feedback.right: Attention lets the representation of "it" draw more heavily from "animal", which is how the model resolves the reference.
feedback.wrong: Attention gives more weight to the relevant context words, here "animal", when building the representation of "it". Equal weights would lose that link.

questions.text: A developer increases the number of attention heads in a Transformer and notices that the model can capture different relationships between tokens. Which explanation is most appropriate?
options: Each head stores a completely separate language model
Different attention heads can learn different patterns or relationships in the representation space
More heads eliminate the need for feed-forward layers
Every head must produce exactly the same attention weights
questions.explain: Multi-head attention allows multiple relationship patterns to be modeled.

feedback.right: Each head has its own learned projections, so one might track syntax while another tracks references.
feedback.wrong: Different heads learn different relationships, such as grammar in one and references in another. They aren't separate models and don't replace feed-forward layers.

questions.text: What generally happens when the value of K in KNN is increased substantially?
options: The prediction becomes influenced by a larger neighborhood and is generally less sensitive to individual nearby points
The model becomes equivalent to Linear Regression
Every training point receives the same class automatically
questions.explain: Larger K creates a broader neighborhood.

feedback.right: A larger K averages over more neighbours, so single noisy points matter less (too large and it underfits).
feedback.wrong: A larger K looks at a bigger neighbourhood, so predictions become smoother and less sensitive to individual points. KNN still uses distances.

questions.text: What is the primary purpose of the attention mechanism in a Transformer?
options: To reduce the number of tokens before processing
To determine how strongly each token should relate to other tokens when creating its contextual representation
To convert every token directly into a class label
To remove the need for embeddings
questions.explain: Attention captures relationships between tokens.

feedback.right: Attention scores how much each token should draw on every other token when building its contextual meaning.
feedback.wrong: Attention decides how strongly each token relates to the others when building its representation. It doesn't remove tokens or replace embeddings.

questions.text: A Transformer model has learned strong relationships between words but produces poor results when token order is changed. Which architectural component helps address this issue?
options: Positional information added to token representations
questions.explain: Self-attention alone does not inherently encode sequence order.

feedback.right: Self-attention has no built-in sense of order, so positional encodings are added to the token embeddings.
feedback.wrong: Add positional information, i.e. positional encodings. On its own, self-attention treats the input as an unordered set of tokens.

questions.text: A Transformer receives a long document and must determine which earlier sentence is relevant to a token near the end. What is the key advantage of self-attention in this situation?
options: It guarantees that every token receives equal importance
It removes all irrelevant tokens before inference
It uses K-Means to identify important sentences
It can directly model relationships between the current token and relevant tokens across the available context
questions.explain: Self-attention enables direct contextual interactions.

feedback.right: Every token can attend directly to any earlier token in the context, however far back it is.
feedback.wrong: Self-attention links the current token directly to relevant tokens anywhere in the context. It doesn't give equal importance or delete tokens.

questions.text: A Transformer processes the sentence "I went to the bank to deposit money." Why might the representation of "bank" differ from its representation in "I sat near the river bank"?
options: Attention allows the token representation to incorporate surrounding contextual information
The model changes the spelling of the token
Linear Regression determines the meaning of the word
questions.explain: Contextual representations depend on surrounding tokens.

feedback.right: The vector for bank is built with attention to its neighbours (deposit, money vs river), so it changes with context.
feedback.wrong: Attention mixes in surrounding context, so bank near "deposit money" gets a different representation than bank near "river". The token itself is the same.

questions.text: In K-Means clustering, what does the centroid represent?
options: The most frequently occurring data point
The representative mean position of the points assigned to a cluster
The closest point to every other cluster
The class label assigned by the model
questions.explain: Centroids represent cluster centers.

feedback.right: A centroid is the mean of all points in its cluster, the cluster's centre.
feedback.wrong: The centroid is the mean position of the points assigned to the cluster. It's usually not an actual data point, and it isn't a class label.

questions.text: A data scientist chooses K=3 for K-Means and observes that several unrelated groups of customers have been merged together. Which action is most reasonable?
options: Evaluate different values of K using appropriate clustering analysis rather than assuming K=3 is optimal
Increase the learning rate because K-Means is a neural network
Reduce the number of features without checking their relevance

feedback.right: K is a guess until tested. The elbow method or silhouette scores help pick a better one.
feedback.wrong: Try different values of K and compare them, for example with the elbow method or silhouette score. K-Means has no learning rate, and dropping features blindly isn't a fix.

questions.text: Which distance measure is commonly used to determine similarity between a data point and a K-Means centroid?
questions.explain: Euclidean distance is commonly used in standard K-Means.

feedback.right: Standard K-Means assigns each point to the nearest centroid by Euclidean distance.
feedback.wrong: Standard K-Means uses Euclidean distance. Cosine, Hamming and Jaccard are used in other settings, such as text or binary data.

questions.text: KNN makes a prediction primarily by:
options: Learning a fixed mathematical equation during training
Examining the nearest training examples and using their labels or values to make a prediction
Training a neural network on the dataset

feedback.right: KNN has no real training step. At prediction time it finds the closest examples and votes or averages their labels.
feedback.wrong: KNN looks at the nearest training examples and uses their labels (a vote) or values (an average). It doesn't learn an equation or build centroids.

questions.text: A KNN model achieves poor performance even after increasing K. Inspection shows that one feature has a much larger scale than all other features and dominates the distance calculation. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: Increasing K alone should always solve feature-scale problems
The distance metric is being distorted by feature scale, so preprocessing should be addressed before further tuning K
KNN cannot be used for classification
The model should be converted into Linear Regression
questions.explain: Feature scaling is fundamental for distance-based algorithms.

feedback.right: No K can fix a distorted distance. Scale the features first, then tune K.
feedback.wrong: The feature scale is distorting distances, so fix the preprocessing (scaling) before tuning K. Changing K doesn't change how distances are calculated.

questions.text: A dataset contains house sizes and corresponding prices. After training Linear Regression, the model consistently underestimates prices for very large houses. What does this most likely suggest?
options: The linear relationship may not adequately represent the relationship across the entire range of house sizes
K-Means has selected the wrong centroid
KNN must always be used instead
The attention mechanism has insufficient context
questions.explain: Model assumptions affect regression performance.

feedback.right: A consistent miss at one end of the range means a straight line doesn't fit the true curve well.
feedback.wrong: A systematic error for large houses suggests the relationship isn't linear across the whole range. Try polynomial features, a log transform or a non-linear model.

questions.text: A team feeds the sentence "The bank approved the loan" into an embedding model. The resulting vector should ideally capture:
options: Only the number of characters in the sentence
Only the position of the word "bank"
Semantic information that can help distinguish the meaning of the sentence from unrelated text
questions.explain: Embeddings encode useful semantic representations.

feedback.right: A sentence embedding captures meaning, so it lands near related text and far from unrelated text.
feedback.wrong: An embedding should capture semantic meaning, which lets you tell this sentence apart from unrelated text. It isn't a character count or a single label.

questions.text: A K-Means model is trained on customer data containing annual income and spending score. Income ranges from 20,000 to 500,000 while spending score ranges from 1 to 100. The resulting clusters are dominated by income. What is the most appropriate improvement?
options: Increase the number of iterations indefinitely
Scale the features so that their numerical ranges do not disproportionately influence distance calculations
Replace every centroid with a random customer
questions.explain: Distance-based algorithms are sensitive to feature scale.

feedback.right: Standardising both features puts them on a comparable scale, so spending score can shape the clusters too.
feedback.wrong: Scale the features, for example with StandardScaler. Income's big range dominates Euclidean distance; more iterations or dropping a feature won't fix that.

questions.text: In Linear Regression, the model attempts to learn:
options: A probability distribution over classes only
A relationship between input features and a continuous numerical target
questions.explain: Linear Regression predicts continuous values.

feedback.right: Linear Regression fits weights linking the features to a continuous number.
feedback.wrong: Linear Regression learns a relationship between features and a continuous target. Clusters belong to K-Means, and nearest examples belong to KNN.

questions.text: In a Transformer, embeddings are mainly used to:
options: Represent tokens as numerical vectors that capture useful semantic information
questions.explain: Embeddings convert discrete tokens into numerical representations.

feedback.right: Embeddings turn token IDs into dense vectors where similar meanings sit close together.
feedback.wrong: Embeddings represent tokens as numerical vectors that carry meaning. Attention then works on those vectors; it isn't replaced by them.

questions.text: Which statement best describes the main advantage of Transformers over traditional sequential RNN processing?
options: Transformers can process token relationships in parallel using attention rather than processing every token strictly one after another
Transformers do not require any numerical representation of text
Transformers always use fewer parameters than RNNs
Transformers eliminate the need for training data
questions.explain: Parallel attention is a major Transformer advantage.

feedback.right: Attention looks at all token pairs at once, so training runs in parallel instead of step by step as in an RNN.
feedback.wrong: The big advantage is parallelism: attention relates all tokens at once instead of one step at a time. Transformers still need numbers and data, and they're often larger.

questions.text: A regression model predicts house prices using only house area. The residual plot shows a clear curved pattern rather than random scatter around zero. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: The model is definitely perfectly fitted
A simple linear relationship may be missing an important non-linear pattern in the data
The dataset must contain duplicate rows
questions.explain: Residual patterns can reveal model inadequacy.

feedback.right: Residuals should scatter randomly around zero. A curved pattern means the straight line is missing a non-linear trend.
feedback.wrong: A curved residual pattern shows the linear model is missing a non-linear relationship. A good fit leaves random scatter around zero.

questions.text: Why are Q, K, and V vectors used in self-attention?
options: To calculate only the model's final loss
To separately store training, testing, and validation data
To determine what a token is looking for, what other tokens offer for matching, and what information should be aggregated
questions.explain: Q, K, and V have distinct roles in attention.

feedback.right: The query is what a token looks for, keys are what others offer to match, and values are the information that gets mixed in.
feedback.wrong: Q is what a token is looking for, K is what each token offers for matching, and V is the content that gets combined. They have nothing to do with dataset splits.

questions.text: A K-Means system is run twice on the same dataset with the same K, but produces different clusters. The implementation initializes centroids randomly. Which explanation is most appropriate?
options: Different initial centroid positions can lead the algorithm toward different local solutions
K-Means always changes the number of clusters automatically
Euclidean distance changes randomly during every iteration
The data must have been converted into embeddings
questions.explain: K-Means can depend on initialization.

feedback.right: K-Means only finds a local optimum, so different starting centroids can end in different clusters. Fix the random seed or use k-means++.
feedback.wrong: Random starting centroids can lead to different local solutions. K stays fixed, and the distance metric doesn't change. Set a seed or use k-means++ with several runs.

questions.text:
```
import numpy as np

a = np.array([[1], [2], [3]])
b = np.array([10, 20])
print(a + b)
```
What is the output?

feedback.right: Shape (3,1) plus shape (2,) broadcasts to (3,2): each row value is added to both 10 and 20.
feedback.wrong: It's [[11, 21], [12, 22], [13, 23]]. Broadcasting stretches the (3,1) column and the (2,) row into a (3,2) grid, so there's no error.

questions.text: A large CSV contains 20 million rows and cannot comfortably fit into memory. Which Pandas approach is most appropriate for computing aggregate statistics?
options: Load the complete file into memory multiple times
Process the CSV incrementally using chunks and combine partial aggregates
Convert it to a larger CSV first

feedback.right: read_csv(chunksize=...) streams the file, so you aggregate each chunk and combine the partial results.
feedback.wrong: Read the file in chunks (read_csv with chunksize) and combine partial aggregates, such as sums and counts for a mean. Loading all 20 million rows at once is the problem.

questions.text: A Pandas DataFrame joins transactions to customer metadata. Customer ID is duplicated in the metadata table even though the business rule says it should be unique. The join multiplies transaction rows. What should be done first?
options: Validate key uniqueness/cardinality and resolve duplicate customer records before joining

feedback.right: Check that the key is really unique first (e.g. merge with validate="many_to_one"), otherwise duplicates multiply rows silently.
feedback.wrong: Validate the key's uniqueness and fix the duplicate customers before joining. Duplicate keys in the lookup table are why the transaction rows multiplied.

questions.text: Two vectors are `[1, 2, 3]` and `[2, 4, 6]`. Under cosine similarity, what relationship should the retrieval system infer?
options: They have cosine similarity 0 because their magnitudes differ
They have cosine similarity -1 because their values are positive
They cannot be compared because their magnitudes differ
They have cosine similarity 1 because they point in the same direction

feedback.right: [2,4,6] is exactly twice [1,2,3], same direction, so the cosine similarity is 1.
feedback.wrong: Their cosine similarity is 1. Cosine only measures direction, and [2,4,6] points the same way as [1,2,3]; the difference in length is ignored.

questions.text: A 10,000-token document must be supplied to a model with a 4,000-token context window. The prompt itself consumes 500 tokens. What is the maximum approximate token budget available for retrieved document context?

feedback.right: 4,000 total minus 500 for the prompt leaves about 3,500 tokens for retrieved context.
feedback.wrong: About 3,500 tokens: the 4,000-token window minus the 500-token prompt. In practice also reserve room for the model's answer.

questions.text: A retrieval corpus contains documents in two versions. Old chunks and current chunks have identical text for some sections, but the application must return only the current version. What metadata enables reliable filtering?
options: Document/source version metadata associated with each chunk

feedback.right: Version metadata on each chunk lets you filter to the current version even when the text is identical.
feedback.wrong: Store document version metadata with each chunk and filter on it. Identical text means only metadata can tell old chunks from current ones.

questions.text: A RAG application retrieves relevant chunks from several documents but provides no source attribution in the final answer. Which pipeline change most directly enables traceability?
options: Preserve source/document metadata through retrieval and expose citations or source references in the generation layer

feedback.right: Keep source metadata with each chunk through retrieval so the answer can cite exactly where it came from.
feedback.wrong: Carry source and document metadata through retrieval and show citations in the answer. Bigger embeddings or random ordering don't make answers traceable.

questions.text: A GenAI pipeline logs `API_KEY=...` whenever an embedding request fails. What is the correct security response?
options: Redact secrets from logs and rotate any credential that was exposed
Base64-encode the key in future logs
Duplicate the key in debug logs

feedback.right: Remove the secret from logs and rotate the key, since anyone who saw the logs could have copied it.
feedback.wrong: Redact secrets from logs and rotate the exposed key. Base64 isn't encryption, and longer retention keeps the leak around longer.

questions.text: A keyword retriever scores a chunk by raw count of query-term occurrences. A chunk repeats the same sentence 50 times and ranks above a concise highly relevant chunk. Which refinement is most appropriate?
options: Use normalized or capped term-frequency scoring and evaluate relevance beyond raw repetition

feedback.right: Capping or normalising term frequency (as BM25 does) stops repeated text from gaming the score.
feedback.wrong: Use normalised or capped term frequency, as BM25 does, and judge relevance beyond repetition. Raw counts reward spam that repeats words.

questions.text: A unit test for a text chunking function unexpectedly calls a real embedding API and becomes slow and nondeterministic. What design change is most appropriate?
options: Call the real API more times
Inject or mock the embedding dependency so the unit test isolates chunking behavior

feedback.right: Mocking or injecting the embedding client keeps the unit test fast and deterministic, and focused only on chunking.
feedback.wrong: Mock or inject the embedding dependency. A unit test should check chunking alone, not hit a real API that is slow and changes its output.

questions.text: A DataFrame contains `amount` values such as `"1200.50"`, `"N/A"`, and `"unknown"`. The pipeline must calculate a numeric median. Which approach is correct?
options: Convert every invalid value to its string length
Sort the strings and take the middle string
Convert with numeric coercion and explicitly handle non-convertible values before computing the median

feedback.right: pd.to_numeric(errors="coerce") turns N/A and unknown into NaN, which median() skips, but decide explicitly how to handle them.
feedback.wrong: Coerce to numbers (pd.to_numeric with errors="coerce") and handle the invalid values deliberately. The median of strings has no numeric meaning.

questions.text: A data-quality rule says the batch must fail if more than 20% of documents cannot be parsed. Which implementation matches the rule?
options: Track parse failures, calculate the failure ratio, and fail the batch when the ratio exceeds 20%
Stop after the first failed document

feedback.right: Counting failures and failing only when the ratio passes 20% matches the rule exactly.
feedback.wrong: Track failures, compute the failure ratio, and fail the batch only when it exceeds 20%. Stopping at the first failure is stricter than the rule.

questions.text: Two normalized embedding vectors are `[0.6, 0.8]` and `[0.8, 0.6]`. What is their cosine similarity?

feedback.right: For normalised vectors cosine similarity is the dot product: 0.6×0.8 + 0.8×0.6 = 0.96.
feedback.wrong: It's 0.96. Both vectors have length 1, so cosine equals the dot product: 0.48 + 0.48. 0.48 is only half of that sum.

questions.text: A function accepts configuration and directly accesses `config['chunk_size']`. Missing configuration causes a KeyError deep inside the pipeline. What is the strongest improvement?
options: Validate required configuration at the application boundary and raise a descriptive configuration error

feedback.right: Checking config at startup fails fast with a clear message, instead of a confusing KeyError deep in the pipeline.
feedback.wrong: Validate required config at the entry point and raise a clear configuration error. Suppressing KeyErrors or using random defaults hides the real problem.

questions.text:
A document contains 2,500 tokens. The chunk size is 600 tokens and the overlap is 100 tokens.

The starting position of each new chunk advances by:

600 − 100 = 500 tokens

How many chunks are required to cover the document?

feedback.right: Chunks start at 0, 500, 1000, 1500 and 2000. The fifth one reaches the end at 2500.
feedback.wrong: Five chunks. Starts at 0, 500, 1000, 1500 and 2000; four chunks only reach token 2100, so a fifth is needed to cover up to 2500.

questions.text: A retrieval system returns highly relevant chunks, but the generated answer frequently ignores the retrieved evidence. Which conclusion is technically justified?
options: Retrieval quality is acceptable, but generation/context-use behavior requires separate evaluation
The vector database must be corrupt
The embeddings must be zero vectors

feedback.right: Good retrieval plus bad answers points at the generation step, so evaluate them separately (faithfulness, grounding).
feedback.wrong: Retrieval is fine, so the problem is in generation or how the context is used, which needs its own evaluation. Nothing suggests a corrupt index or zero vectors.

feedback.right: An inner merge pairs each left row with every matching right row: id 1 matches two rows and id 2 matches one, giving 3.
feedback.wrong: It prints 3. id 1 appears twice on the right, so it produces two rows; id 2 produces one. Merges multiply rows on duplicate keys.

questions.text: A Python module executes the entire document-ingestion pipeline as soon as another module imports it. A test importing one helper unexpectedly starts ingestion. Which change is appropriate?
options: Move ingestion into a module-level loop
Place executable entry-point logic behind functions and an `if __name__ == '__main__':` guard
Run ingestion from every helper function

feedback.right: Wrapping the pipeline in a function behind the __main__ guard means importing the module never starts ingestion.
feedback.wrong: Put the pipeline in functions and call them only under if __name__ == '__main__':. Module-level code runs on every import.

questions.text: A custom exception represents invalid user configuration, while a database timeout represents infrastructure failure. Why should they use different exception types?
options: Different exception types allow callers to apply different handling, retry, alerting, and user-facing behavior
Only custom exceptions can be logged
Python requires every exception to have a unique filename

feedback.right: Separate types let callers catch each one differently: show a config error to the user, retry and alert on the timeout.
feedback.wrong: Different types let callers handle each case differently, such as retrying a timeout but reporting bad config to the user. They don't change speed or logging.

questions.text: A pipeline derives daily metrics from timestamps arriving in UTC, IST, and EST. Grouping directly by local date produces inconsistent daily counts. What should happen first?
options: Drop all timezone information without a policy
Normalize timestamps to a defined reference timezone before deriving the grouping date

feedback.right: Convert every timestamp to one reference timezone first; only then is 'the date' consistent.
feedback.wrong: Normalise all timestamps to one reference timezone (often UTC) before deriving the date. Mixed zones put the same moment on different days.

questions.text: A chunk is 800 tokens, while the model's remaining context budget after system instructions and user query is 650 tokens. What must the RAG pipeline do?
options: Send all 800 tokens because chunk size is independent of prompt size
Retrieve or truncate/rechunk context so the final prompt remains within the available context budget

feedback.right: The whole prompt must fit the window, so trim, re-chunk or pick smaller pieces to stay within the 650 tokens left.
feedback.wrong: Retrieve less, truncate or re-chunk so the prompt fits the 650 tokens left. The context limit is fixed; anything over it gets cut off or rejected.

questions.text: A NumPy array `x` has shape `(100,1)` and `y` has shape `(1,50)`. What is the shape of `x + y` under broadcasting?

feedback.right: (100,1) and (1,50) both stretch along their size-1 axes, giving (100,50).
feedback.wrong: The result is (100, 50). Each size-1 dimension stretches to match the other array, so the column and the row form a full grid.

questions.text: A dataset has a feature with 45% missing values. Replacing all missing values with zero changes the distribution substantially. What should be evaluated before selecting an imputation method?
options: The missingness mechanism, feature semantics, and downstream modeling impact

feedback.right: Why values are missing, what the feature means, and how the model will use it all decide the right imputation.
feedback.wrong: Look at why the data is missing, what the feature means and how imputation affects the model. Zero-filling 45% of a column badly skews its distribution.

questions.text: A simulated embedding function averages token vectors. A document contains no recognized tokens after preprocessing. What should robust code do?
options: Use the document ID as the vector
Divide by zero and suppress the error
Return a random vector without logging
Handle the empty-vector case explicitly rather than calculating an invalid mean

feedback.right: An empty token list would mean dividing by zero, so handle it explicitly: skip, flag or log the document.
feedback.wrong: Handle the empty case explicitly. Averaging zero vectors divides by zero, and a silent random vector corrupts search results.

questions.text: A RAG system stores embeddings but not source text or document metadata. Retrieval returns vector IDs but cannot construct a meaningful context. What should each indexed item retain?
options: Chunk text plus stable source/document metadata

feedback.right: Retrieval needs to return text the model can read, plus metadata for citations and filtering.
feedback.wrong: Store the chunk text and stable source metadata with each vector. A vector ID alone gives the model nothing it can read.

questions.text: A NumPy array has shape `(1000, 20)` and contains 1,000 observations with 20 features. The analyst needs one mean value per feature across observations. Which axis should be used?

feedback.right: axis=0 collapses the rows (observations), leaving one mean per column: 20 values.
feedback.wrong: Use axis=0, which aggregates down the rows and gives 20 feature means. axis=1 would give 1,000 per-row means, and there is no axis 2 in a 2-D array.

questions.text: A Python data pipeline processes each document independently. One malformed document should be logged and skipped while all other documents continue. Where should the exception boundary be placed?
options: Around the per-document processing operation, with document-specific logging and controlled continuation
Around the entire batch with immediate termination

feedback.right: A try/except around each document logs the bad one and lets the loop carry on.
feedback.wrong: Put the try/except around each document's processing, log the failure and continue. Wrapping the whole batch stops everything at the first bad file.

questions.text: A data-cleaning function mutates a DataFrame supplied by its caller. Another component unexpectedly sees the changes. What is the underlying issue?
options: Python automatically clones every DataFrame argument
The function is mutating a shared mutable object; copying or an explicit mutation contract is needed

feedback.right: DataFrames are mutable and passed by reference, so in-place changes are visible to everyone holding the same object.
feedback.wrong: The function mutates a shared, mutable object. Python passes a reference, not a copy, so return a modified copy or document that it mutates.

questions.text: A RAG ingestion pipeline processes 20,000 documents. Re-running ingestion currently recomputes embeddings for every document. Which design most directly enables incremental ingestion?
options: Delete the entire vector index before every ingestion
Use the document filename length as the ID
Track stable document IDs and content/version hashes and re-embed only changed documents
Generate random IDs on every run

feedback.right: Stable IDs plus content hashes show which documents changed, so only those are re-embedded.
feedback.wrong: Track stable document IDs and content hashes, and re-embed only what changed. Random IDs or wiping the index force everything to be redone.

questions.text: A Pandas filter needs rows where `score >= 0.8` AND `status == 'approved'`. Which implementation concept is correct for Series-level conditions?
options: Convert the DataFrame to JSON first
Combine boolean Series using element-wise logical operators such as `&`, with each condition parenthesized

feedback.right: Pandas needs element-wise & with each condition in parentheses: (df.score >= 0.8) & (df.status == 'approved').
feedback.wrong: Use & between parenthesised boolean Series. Python's and tries to get one True/False from a whole Series and raises a ValueError.

questions.text: A tokenized sentence is represented as a matrix where each row is a token vector. The application needs one mean vector representing all tokens. Which operation is appropriate?
options: Use np.mean(array, axis=0) to average token vectors
Use np.mean(array, axis=1) to average vector components
Use np.sum(array, axis=2) to combine token representations
Use np.max(array, axis=3) to select the strongest token values

feedback.right: Rows are tokens, so axis=0 averages down the rows and gives one vector with the embedding's width.
feedback.wrong: Use np.mean(array, axis=0). It averages across the token rows and keeps every vector dimension; axis=1 would give one number per token instead.

questions.text: A keyword retriever ranks documents by counting matching query terms. What problem can occur when raw counts are used without normalization?
options: Every query can receive the same score across documents
Long or repetitive documents may receive inflated rankings
Embedding vectors can become random during retrieval
No document can be returned when a query contains terms

feedback.right: Raw counts reward length and repetition, so long or spammy documents rank too high.
feedback.wrong: Long or repetitive documents get inflated scores, because more words means more matches. Normalising by length (as BM25 does) fixes this.

questions.text: A customer reference DataFrame contains duplicate customer IDs before it is joined to a transaction DataFrame. What should be checked first?
options: Check the index formatting used by the reference table
Check the file extension used by the source dataset
Check the ordering of columns in both DataFrames
Check whether the customer key is unique

feedback.right: If the key isn't unique, the join duplicates transaction rows, so check uniqueness before anything else.
feedback.wrong: Check whether the customer key is unique. Duplicate keys in the reference table multiply the joined rows; formatting and column order don't matter.

questions.text: A NumPy array has shape (5, 3), where rows represent documents and columns represent features. A reduction uses axis=0. What does the reduction operate across?
options: It reduces across both dimensions of the array
It reduces across the feature columns of each document
It avoids reducing either dimension of the array
It reduces across the document rows for each feature

feedback.right: axis=0 collapses the rows, so you get one result per feature column, computed across all documents.
feedback.wrong: axis=0 reduces down the document rows, giving one value per feature. Reducing across the feature columns of each document would be axis=1.

questions.text: An AI application needs a named error specifically for an unsupported document format. Which statement best describes the role of a custom exception?
options: A named error type for a specific application condition
A replacement for application logging during failures
A faster form of inheritance used by the processing pipeline
A mechanism for storing embeddings associated with an input

feedback.right: A custom exception names a specific failure (UnsupportedFormatError) so callers can catch and handle exactly that case.
feedback.wrong: A custom exception is a named error type for one specific condition. It doesn't replace logging, and it has nothing to do with speed or storing data.

questions.text: A retrieved RAG chunk is too large to fit within the model’s remaining context budget. What should the pipeline do?
options: Send the complete chunk despite the context limit
Delete the user query to make additional space
Increase the embedding vector size to fit the context
Reduce or re-chunk the retrieved context before generation

feedback.right: Shrink or re-chunk the context so the whole prompt fits. Anything past the limit is cut or rejected.
feedback.wrong: Reduce or re-chunk the retrieved text before generating. Sending it anyway overflows the context, and deleting the user's query defeats the purpose.

questions.text: A text-cleaning function should remove leading and trailing spaces. Which assertion directly verifies the expected result for clean(' text ')?

feedback.right: The assertion checks the exact expected output: both outer spaces gone, leaving 'text'.
feedback.wrong: Assert clean(' text ') == 'text'. That checks the exact result: leading and trailing spaces removed and the word kept.

questions.text: A RAG index stores embedding vectors and numeric IDs. Retrieval returns the IDs, but the application cannot build the context sent to the model. What is missing?
options: The chunk text and source metadata associated with the IDs
A second Python interpreter for the retrieval pipeline
A larger display area for showing the retrieved results
A classification label attached to each retrieved chunk

feedback.right: Vector IDs alone are meaningless to the LLM. You need the chunk text (and source info) to build the prompt.
feedback.wrong: The chunk text and its source metadata are missing. Retrieval gives IDs, but the model needs actual text to read and sources to cite.

questions.text: A BaseAgent class defines run(), while several specialized agents provide their own implementations of run(). Which OOP concept does this design demonstrate?
options: Aggregation combines the agents into one workflow
Iteration repeats the same run() implementation
Inheritance requires every agent to use identical run() logic

feedback.right: Calling agent.run() works on any agent, and each subclass runs its own version. That's polymorphism.
feedback.wrong: It's polymorphism: one run() interface with a different implementation in each agent. Inheritance doesn't force identical logic; overriding is what lets them differ.

questions.text: An AI application reads configuration settings before starting document processing. Why is it useful to keep configuration handling separate from processing logic?
options: It removes the need to test the processing pipeline
It guarantees that every supplied input is valid
It improves separation of concerns between responsibilities
It eliminates the possibility of exceptions during processing

feedback.right: Keeping config separate from processing gives each part one job, which makes both easier to change and test.
feedback.wrong: It improves separation of concerns. It doesn't validate every input or prevent exceptions; it just keeps two responsibilities apart.

questions.text: A developer is investigating why an AI pipeline produces an unexpected embedding during development. Which logging level is generally most appropriate for detailed diagnostic information?
options: OFF prevents unnecessary messages during processing
CRITICAL records the most detailed processing information

feedback.right: DEBUG is the most detailed level and is meant for diagnosing problems during development.
feedback.wrong: Use DEBUG for detailed diagnostic output. ERROR and CRITICAL are for failures and record less detail, and OFF records nothing.

questions.text: A keyword-based retriever should treat the terms AI, Ai, and ai as equivalent during matching. What is the primary purpose of lowercasing the text?
options: Reduce retrieval differences caused by letter case
Create dense embeddings from the normalized text
Preserve the original capitalization of every term
Increase the length of the processed document text

feedback.right: Lowercasing makes AI, Ai and ai the same token, so letter case no longer affects matching.
feedback.wrong: The goal is to remove differences caused by letter case. Lowercasing doesn't create embeddings and it deliberately throws away the original capitalisation.

questions.text: A unit test for a chunking function calls a live external API every time it runs. Why is this undesirable for a unit test?
options: It makes the chunking operation impossible to test
It makes the test slower and less deterministic
It guarantees higher code coverage for the function
It removes the need to use assertions in the test

feedback.right: Network calls are slow and their responses can change, so the test becomes slow and flaky.
feedback.wrong: It makes the test slower and non-deterministic, since results depend on the network and the API. The chunking can still be tested; mock the API instead.

questions.text: During testing, an API token accidentally appears in an application log. What should the logging code do before recording the message?
options: Repeat the token once so the failure can be traced
Increase log verbosity so the surrounding event is clearer
Encode the token with Base64 before writing the log
Redact the sensitive value before writing the log

feedback.right: Redact the token before writing the log, e.g. replace it with ***. Logs are often widely readable.
feedback.wrong: Redact the sensitive value before logging. Base64 is trivially reversible, and repeating the token or logging more just spreads the leak.

questions.text: A large CSV file is too large to load comfortably into memory as one DataFrame. Which Pandas approach is appropriate?
options: Convert every row to JSON before loading the dataset
Load the complete CSV repeatedly to reduce memory use
Print the complete file while processing each record
Read the CSV in manageable chunks during processing

feedback.right: pd.read_csv(..., chunksize=N) gives you manageable pieces you can process one at a time.
feedback.wrong: Read the CSV in chunks with chunksize. Loading it repeatedly or converting rows to JSON only adds memory and work.

questions.text: A RAG system compares two normalized embedding vectors that point in exactly the same direction. What cosine similarity should the system obtain?

feedback.right: Vectors pointing the same way have an angle of 0, and cos(0) = 1.
feedback.wrong: It should be 1. Cosine similarity measures the angle; same direction means angle 0 and cos 0 = 1. -1 is opposite and 0 is unrelated (orthogonal).

questions.text: A reusable AI pipeline contains several repeated processing steps. Which practice most directly improves its code quality and maintainability?
options: Use global variables for all configuration settings
Use small functions with clear responsibilities
Place every processing step inside one large function
Duplicate similar logic across separate application modules

feedback.right: Small single-purpose functions are easy to read, reuse and test, and remove duplicated steps.
feedback.wrong: Use small functions with clear responsibilities. One giant function, global config and copy-pasted logic all make the pipeline harder to change.

questions.text: A retrieval system removes common stopwords from every document and query. Why might this be unsuitable for some retrieval tasks?
options: Stopwords are always longer than important keywords
Stopwords cannot be tokenized correctly by retrieval systems
Some stopwords can contribute to the meaning of a query
Stopwords always contain numerical information in documents

feedback.right: Words like 'not', 'without' or 'to be or not to be' can change meaning entirely, so dropping them can hurt.
feedback.wrong: Some stopwords carry meaning, like 'not' in 'not refundable'. Removing them blindly can flip what a query is asking.

questions.text: A Pandas column contains the values '10', '25', and 'unknown'. Before calculating a numeric average, which approach is suitable?
options: Use pd.to_numeric with coercion for nonnumeric values
Sort the values alphabetically and calculate the average
Convert the numeric strings into separate Python lists
Concatenate all values into one string before averaging

feedback.right: pd.to_numeric(errors='coerce') turns 'unknown' into NaN, and mean() skips NaN by default.
feedback.wrong: Use pd.to_numeric with errors='coerce'. Non-numbers become NaN and are skipped by mean(); sorting or concatenating strings gives no average.

questions.text: A developer writes a text-cleaning function that should remove extra spaces. What is the main purpose of a unit test for this function?
options: Replace application logging for the supplied test input
Verify one specific behavior of the function in isolation
Train an embedding model using the cleaned text
Measure production traffic generated by the function

feedback.right: A unit test checks one behaviour of one function in isolation, with a known input and expected output.
feedback.wrong: A unit test verifies one specific behaviour of the function in isolation. It doesn't train models, replace logging or measure production traffic.

questions.text: A developer needs the average value of every element in a NumPy array before passing the result to another calculation. Which operation should be used?
options: Use np.mean() to calculate the overall average
Use np.reshape() to change the array structure
Use np.unique() to return distinct array values
Use np.stack() to combine arrays along an axis

feedback.right: np.mean() with no axis averages every element in the array.
feedback.wrong: Use np.mean() without an axis to average all elements. reshape changes the shape, unique finds distinct values, and stack joins arrays.

questions.text: A 2,000-token document is split into 500-token chunks with 100-token overlap. What does the overlap primarily provide for the RAG pipeline?
options: It automatically filters metadata from each document chunk
It reduces the number of chunks created from the document
It increases the embedding dimension of every chunk
It preserves shared context between adjacent chunks

feedback.right: Overlap repeats the edge of one chunk at the start of the next, so ideas split at a boundary stay together.
feedback.wrong: Overlap preserves shared context between neighbouring chunks. It actually adds chunks, and it has no effect on metadata or embedding size.

questions.text: A DataFrame should keep rows where score is at least 0.8 and status equals 'approved'. Which expression correctly applies both conditions?

feedback.right: Each condition is in parentheses and combined with &, which is how pandas does element-wise AND.
feedback.wrong: Use (df['score'] >= 0.8) & (df['status'] == 'approved'). and/or fail on whole Series, and without parentheses & binds before the comparisons.

questions.text: An embedding job fails for one document, and the developer needs to identify that document without exposing confidential content. What should be included in the log?
options: Only the Python version used by the application
A safe identifier that identifies the document
The complete API secret used during processing
The complete contents of the document that failed

feedback.right: A safe ID (like a document ID or hash) pinpoints the failure without leaking the content.
feedback.wrong: Log a safe identifier such as the document ID. Logging the content leaks confidential data, and logging the API secret is worse.

questions.text: A simple keyword retriever treats punctuation as separate token variations. A preprocessing step removes punctuation before retrieval. What is a possible benefit?
options: It reduces superficial token variations during matching
It guarantees semantic similarity between retrieved texts
It creates contextual embeddings from the cleaned sentence
It increases the vocabulary size used during retrieval

feedback.right: Stripping punctuation makes 'error,' and 'error' the same token, so trivial variations stop blocking matches.
feedback.wrong: It reduces superficial token variations, so 'error.' matches 'error'. It doesn't create semantic understanding and it shrinks the vocabulary rather than growing it.

questions.text: A RAG system returns excellent documents for each individual query, but the final context contains repeated versions of the same information. Which improvement is most appropriate?
options: Increase the number of retrieval sources without deduplication
Deduplicate or diversify the candidate set before constructing the final context
Increase chunk overlap across every document
Increase the model temperature during generation
questions.explain: Retrieval diversity can improve context usefulness.

feedback.right: Removing near-duplicates (or using MMR) frees up context space for different, useful evidence.
feedback.wrong: Deduplicate or diversify the candidates before building the context. More sources, more overlap or a higher temperature add more repetition, not less.

questions.text: Which situation is most suitable for query rewriting?
options: The user's query is vague, incomplete, or poorly aligned with document terminology
The vector database has already returned perfectly ranked documents
The LLM needs a larger number of output tokens
The application needs to change the embedding dimension
questions.explain: Rewriting improves the retrieval formulation.

feedback.right: Rewriting helps when the user's wording is vague or doesn't match the document vocabulary.
feedback.wrong: Query rewriting suits vague, incomplete or mismatched queries. If retrieval is already perfect, rewriting adds nothing; it also doesn't touch output length or embedding size.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of Retrieval-Augmented Generation?
options: To fine-tune a model using every retrieved document
To replace the language model with a search engine
To provide retrieved information as context for grounded generation
To convert documents directly into model parameters
questions.explain: RAG combines retrieval with generation.

feedback.right: RAG retrieves relevant information and gives it to the model as context, so answers are grounded in real sources.
feedback.wrong: RAG supplies retrieved information as context so the model's answer is grounded. It doesn't fine-tune the model or replace it with a search engine.

questions.text: A documentation assistant receives the query "Why isn't it working after I changed the configuration?" The word "it" refers to an API gateway discussed earlier in the conversation. What should happen before retrieval?
options: Remove the previous conversation to avoid retrieval bias
Search for the literal word "it" across the documentation
Replace the query with a generic troubleshooting prompt
Resolve the reference and rewrite the query using the known API gateway context
questions.explain: Conversational references should be resolved before retrieval.

feedback.right: Resolve 'it' to the API gateway and rewrite the query, so retrieval searches for what the user actually means.
feedback.wrong: Resolve the reference using the conversation and rewrite the query around the API gateway. Searching for the literal word 'it' finds nothing useful.

questions.text: Which statement best describes a vector database?
options: A database designed mainly for transactional SQL operations
A database that stores only raw text and metadata
A database that generates answers from stored documents
A system optimized for searching numerical vector representations
questions.explain: Vector databases support similarity-based retrieval.

feedback.right: A vector database indexes embeddings for fast nearest-neighbour (similarity) search.
feedback.wrong: A vector database is built for searching numerical vectors by similarity. It doesn't generate answers, and transactional SQL is a relational database's job.

questions.text: A production search pipeline combines BM25 and dense retrieval. BM25 performs well for product IDs and policy numbers, while dense retrieval performs better for natural-language questions. RRF improves recall, but the final top results still contain near-duplicates. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Increase the RRF constant until duplicate documents disappear
Apply deduplication or diversity-aware selection after fusion and before final context construction
Remove BM25 because duplicates indicate lexical retrieval failure
Increase the embedding dimension of all indexed documents
questions.explain: Fusion combines rankings but does not automatically solve redundancy.

feedback.right: RRF merges rankings but doesn't remove duplicates. Deduplicate or use diversity-aware selection (such as MMR) after fusion.
feedback.wrong: Add deduplication or diversity-aware selection after fusion. Tweaking the RRF constant doesn't remove duplicates, and dropping BM25 loses the exact-ID matches.

questions.text: A company's HR chatbot receives the query: "How many days can I take for parental leave?" The policy documents use the term "parental benefit entitlement period." The current embedding search often misses the relevant section. What should be tested first?
options: Increase the LLM temperature during answer generation
Rewrite the query using terminology closer to the organization's policy language
Remove metadata filters from the vector database
Increase the dimensionality of the embeddings
questions.explain: Query-document terminology mismatch can reduce retrieval quality.

feedback.right: Rewriting the query into the policy's own terms closes the vocabulary gap that makes search miss the section.
feedback.wrong: Test query rewriting first, into the policy's terminology. The problem is a wording mismatch; temperature and embedding size don't change that.

questions.text: A team adds HYDE to a RAG system and observes better recall but more irrelevant results. Which explanation is most reasonable?
options: The hypothetical document may introduce concepts that differ from the user's actual information need
HYDE guarantees semantic precision but reduces database availability
The vector database cannot store hypothetical documents
HYDE changes the source documents during retrieval
questions.explain: HYDE can improve semantic alignment but may introduce retrieval drift.

feedback.right: The hypothetical answer may wander into concepts the user didn't ask about, pulling in off-topic documents.
feedback.wrong: HyDE's generated document can introduce ideas the user didn't mean, so recall rises but precision drops. It doesn't modify the source documents.

questions.text: A RAG architecture currently follows: Query → Dense Retrieval → Top-20 → LLM. Evaluation shows that relevant documents are present in the top-20, but the final answers frequently use lower-quality passages while ignoring stronger evidence. Which redesign is most likely to improve the system without simply increasing the context size?
options: Increase top-k to 100 so the model has more evidence
Increase chunk size so every retrieved result contains more information
Add another embedding model and concatenate all retrieved vectors
Use a candidate-retrieval stage followed by re-ranking, evidence-aware context selection, and grounding validation
questions.explain: Better RAG systems separate recall, ranking, context selection, and grounding.

feedback.right: Separate the steps: retrieve broadly, re-rank, pick the strongest evidence and check grounding, instead of passing all 20.
feedback.wrong: Use candidate retrieval followed by re-ranking, evidence-aware selection and grounding checks. A bigger top-k or bigger chunks add more noise for the model.

questions.text: What is the basic idea behind HYDE?
options: Generate multiple embeddings and average them before retrieval
Retrieve documents first and generate a query from every document
Replace the original query with a keyword-only representation
Generate a hypothetical document and use it to improve semantic retrieval
questions.explain: HYDE uses hypothetical documents for retrieval.

feedback.right: HyDE asks the LLM to write a hypothetical answer, then searches with that answer's embedding.
feedback.wrong: HyDE generates a hypothetical document for the query and uses its embedding for retrieval. It isn't averaging embeddings or a keyword-only query.

questions.text: An enterprise RAG system uses BM25, dense retrieval, query rewriting, RRF, and a cross-encoder. Offline retrieval recall is excellent, but answer accuracy remains poor. Evaluation shows that the top-ranked passages often contain relevant keywords but do not actually contain enough evidence to support the generated claims. What should be investigated first?
options: Increasing the number of retrieval algorithms
Improving final context selection and grounding validation after re-ranking
Replacing BM25 with another lexical ranking algorithm
questions.explain: Retrieval recall does not guarantee sufficient evidence for generation.

feedback.right: Recall is fine; the passages that reach the model lack enough evidence. Fix context selection and add grounding checks.
feedback.wrong: Investigate final context selection and grounding validation after re-ranking. More retrievers won't help when the chosen passages don't support the claims.

questions.text: A technical RAG system retrieves the correct paragraph but also returns several unrelated paragraphs containing the same general keywords. Which approach would most directly improve the final ordering?
options: Increase the number of BM25 results returned
Replace all chunks with larger documents
Increase the LLM temperature before retrieval
Apply a semantic re-ranker to the retrieved candidate set
questions.explain: Re-ranking can improve precision after candidate retrieval.

feedback.right: A semantic re-ranker scores each candidate against the query and pushes the truly relevant paragraph to the top.
feedback.wrong: Apply a semantic re-ranker to the candidates. More BM25 results or bigger chunks add more keyword noise rather than fixing the order.

questions.text: A user asks, "What changed in the authentication process between version 2 and version 3?" The knowledge base contains separate release notes, API documentation, and migration guides. A direct semantic query retrieves mostly version 3 documentation. Which pipeline is most likely to produce a balanced evidence set?
options: Rewrite the query into comparison-focused subqueries, retrieve across relevant sources, fuse rankings, and re-rank the candidates
Increase top-k on the original query and pass every result to the LLM
Use HYDE alone and ignore the original query terminology
Use BM25 alone because version numbers are present in the documents
questions.explain: Comparative questions often benefit from query decomposition and multi-source retrieval.

feedback.right: Splitting the question into v2 and v3 subqueries across the right sources, then fusing and re-ranking, gives balanced evidence.
feedback.wrong: Break it into comparison subqueries, search the relevant sources, fuse and re-rank. A bigger top-k on the original query still returns mostly v3 documents.

questions.text: What does Reciprocal Rank Fusion primarily combine?
options: Ranked result lists produced by different retrieval methods
Chunk vectors generated from different documents
questions.explain: RRF combines rankings rather than embedding vectors.

feedback.right: RRF merges ranked lists using each document's rank position, not its raw score.
feedback.wrong: RRF combines ranked result lists from different retrievers, using rank positions. It doesn't merge embeddings or token probabilities.

questions.text: A RAG application uses 200-token chunks with no overlap. Answers are technically relevant but frequently miss conditions stated at the end of one section and the beginning of the next. What should the team investigate?
options: Introducing appropriate chunk overlap or boundary-aware chunking
Reducing the retrieval top-k to one
questions.explain: Poor boundaries can split related information.

feedback.right: Overlap or boundary-aware chunking keeps conditions that cross a section edge in the same chunk.
feedback.wrong: Add chunk overlap or boundary-aware chunking. Conditions split across chunks get lost; vector size and top-k don't fix where the cut happens.

questions.text: BM25 primarily determines document relevance using:
options: Term frequency, document frequency, and document length
The probability distribution produced by an LLM
questions.explain: BM25 is a lexical retrieval method.

feedback.right: BM25 scores by term frequency, how rare the term is across documents (IDF), and document length.
feedback.wrong: BM25 uses term frequency, document frequency and document length. It's lexical, so it uses no embeddings, attention or LLM probabilities.

questions.text: Why are documents divided into chunks before being stored in a vector database?
options: To create smaller units that can be retrieved independently
To remove semantic information from large documents
To reduce the number of embeddings to exactly one
To convert unstructured documents into relational tables
questions.explain: Chunking creates manageable retrieval units.

feedback.right: Chunks are small, focused units that can be embedded and retrieved on their own.
feedback.wrong: Chunking creates smaller pieces that can be retrieved independently. It keeps the meaning, produces many embeddings (not one), and has nothing to do with tables.

questions.text: A support system needs to retrieve documents containing exact error codes such as AUTH-4017, while also finding semantically related troubleshooting content. Which design is most appropriate?
options: Use dense retrieval only with a larger embedding model
Use BM25 only and rely on keyword overlap
Combine BM25 and dense retrieval and merge their results
Send the original query directly to the LLM without retrieval
questions.explain: Exact identifiers and semantic concepts benefit from different retrieval signals.

feedback.right: BM25 nails exact codes like AUTH-4017, dense retrieval finds related ideas, and merging gets you both.
feedback.wrong: Combine BM25 and dense retrieval and merge the results. Dense alone can miss exact codes, and BM25 alone misses paraphrased troubleshooting text.

questions.text: A RAG application retrieves 10 documents using dense search and 10 using BM25. Their scores cannot be directly compared because the scoring scales differ. Which technique is most appropriate?
options: Reciprocal Rank Fusion can combine their ranked positions
Keep only the BM25 results because they are lexical
Keep only the dense results because they are semantic
questions.explain: RRF works with rankings rather than requiring compatible score scales.

feedback.right: RRF uses rank positions only, so incompatible score scales don't matter.
feedback.wrong: Use Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Averaging raw scores on different scales is meaningless, and keeping just one list throws away half the signal.

questions.text: Which approach is generally considered hybrid retrieval?
options: Using two different LLMs to generate the final response
Using only a larger dense embedding model
Combining lexical retrieval such as BM25 with dense vector retrieval
Combining multiple prompts before sending one request
questions.explain: Hybrid retrieval combines complementary retrieval methods.

feedback.right: Hybrid retrieval combines lexical search (BM25) with dense vector search.
feedback.wrong: Hybrid retrieval means lexical plus dense retrieval, such as BM25 with embeddings. Two LLMs or combined prompts aren't retrieval at all.

questions.text: What is the main role of a re-ranker in a RAG pipeline?
options: Generate additional documents from the user query
Replace the embedding model used during indexing
Reorder retrieved candidates using a stronger relevance model
Increase the maximum context window of the LLM
questions.explain: Re-ranking refines an initial candidate set.

feedback.right: A re-ranker uses a stronger, slower model (often a cross-encoder) to reorder the first-stage candidates.
feedback.wrong: A re-ranker reorders retrieved candidates with a stronger relevance model. It doesn't generate documents or change the embedding model or context window.

questions.text: What is the main trade-off when increasing chunk size?
options: More context per chunk but potentially less precise retrieval
More precise retrieval with no additional context
Lower storage requirements with identical retrieval behavior
Better semantic similarity without changing the embedding model
questions.explain: Chunk size affects context and retrieval precision.

feedback.right: Bigger chunks carry more context but mix several topics, which blurs similarity matching.
feedback.wrong: Larger chunks give more context per chunk but less precise retrieval, because each embedding covers several ideas. It's a trade-off, not a free gain.

questions.text: A knowledge assistant receives a complex query containing several concepts that rarely appear together in the same document. Which retrieval strategy is likely to improve recall?
options: Increase the LLM temperature and generate a longer answer
Retrieve only the top document for maximum precision
Replace the vector database with a relational database
Generate multiple focused queries and combine their retrieved results
questions.explain: Multiple retrieval formulations can improve coverage.

feedback.right: Splitting the question into focused subqueries finds documents for each concept, then the results are merged.
feedback.wrong: Generate several focused queries and combine their results. A single top document can't cover concepts that rarely appear together.

questions.text: A legal RAG system uses large chunks because individual clauses depend heavily on surrounding text. However, retrieval precision has dropped because each chunk contains multiple unrelated clauses. Which architectural change is most defensible?
options: Return every matching chunk and let the LLM decide which text matters
Reduce every chunk to a fixed 50-token size regardless of document structure
Remove overlap so that chunks become independent
Use structure-aware or semantic chunking and evaluate retrieval quality against representative legal queries
questions.explain: Chunking should reflect document structure and information boundaries.

feedback.right: Chunk along the document's structure (clauses and sections) and measure retrieval on real legal queries.
feedback.wrong: Use structure-aware or semantic chunking and test it on representative queries. Fixed 50-token chunks would split dependent clauses apart.

questions.text: A search system first retrieves 50 candidates using a fast vector index and then applies a cross-encoder to rank them. Why is this two-stage design commonly preferred?
options: The cross-encoder is used only to generate embeddings
Vector search cannot return ranked results
Fast retrieval provides broad candidates while the expensive model focuses on a smaller set
The cross-encoder permanently stores the retrieved documents
questions.explain: Two-stage retrieval balances recall, precision, and latency.

feedback.right: The cheap vector search narrows the set quickly, then the costly cross-encoder only scores the 50 candidates.
feedback.wrong: Fast retrieval gathers broad candidates, and the expensive cross-encoder ranks just that small set. Running the cross-encoder on everything would be far too slow.

questions.text: A retail bot recommends discontinued products because the vector store still holds outdated chunks, even after the catalog was updated days ago. Enlarging the context window did not help. Why not?
options: Context window size directly controls how often the vector store gets refreshed
The context window and the vector store are the same component under the hood
The larger window already fixed it, but only for queries under 50 tokens
Context window size cannot fix stale content; the store needs a refresh pipeline instead
questions.explain: Context window size affects how much retrieved text the model can process per call; it has no bearing on whether the retrieved content itself is current. The fix is a refresh pipeline for the index.

feedback.right: The window controls how much text fits per call, not whether that text is current. Stale data needs a re-index pipeline.
feedback.wrong: A bigger context window can't make stale content current; the store needs a refresh pipeline. The window and the vector store are separate components.

questions.text: A researcher agent and a writer agent share a mutable LangGraph state, and a reviewer worries one could silently overwrite the other's data. What is the most accurate response?
options: The risk is real, so state schemas need deliberate keys or reducers to prevent overwrites
The concern is baseless, since no node can ever modify shared state in LangGraph
The concern only applies to BM25 retrieval and has nothing to do with state
The concern is irrelevant, since separate agents never actually run within the same process at all
questions.explain: Shared state is powerful but does carry a real risk of unintended overwrites; careful state schema design (distinct keys, reducer functions, or merge strategies) mitigates this rather than the risk being nonexistent.

feedback.right: Shared state can be overwritten, so use distinct keys or reducers that define how updates merge.
feedback.wrong: The risk is real. Nodes do write to shared state, so design the schema with separate keys or reducer functions to stop one agent overwriting another.

questions.text: A search engineer says BM25 should be replaced everywhere since 'dense embeddings are strictly better.' In which scenario does this advice clearly backfire?
options: When users only describe items in vague, paraphrased language with no specifics
When the entire corpus is small enough to fit inside the model's context window
When the system never needs to rank more than a single document per query
When users search using exact part numbers or SKUs, where lexical overlap matters most
questions.explain: Dense embeddings capture semantic similarity but can under-weight exact token matches like part numbers, where BM25's lexical scoring excels.

feedback.right: Exact identifiers like part numbers or SKUs need lexical matching, which is where BM25 beats embeddings.
feedback.wrong: It backfires on exact part numbers or SKUs. Dense embeddings blur exact tokens, while BM25 matches them precisely. Vague queries are where dense search shines.

questions.text: A colleague argues RAG makes hallucination mathematically impossible because the model 'just reads from the documents.' Why is this reasoning incorrect?
options: RAG only accepts structured databases, so plain text documents cannot be indexed
RAG removes the LLM entirely, leaving no generation step that could hallucinate
Retrieval only supplies context; the LLM still generates text and can misstate it
Retrieval in RAG happens only after the final answer has already been produced
questions.explain: Retrieval supplies grounding context, but generation is still probabilistic; the model can still misinterpret, omit, or contradict retrieved text.

feedback.right: Retrieval only supplies context; the LLM still generates the answer and can misread, omit or contradict it.
feedback.wrong: RAG reduces hallucination but doesn't eliminate it. The LLM still generates text and can misstate what it retrieved.

questions.text: A team benchmarks BM25 against dense retrieval and calls dense 'universally better' after it won on one paraphrase-heavy test set. What is the main risk in generalizing this?
options: There is no risk, since one benchmark result generalizes cleanly to every query type
BM25 cannot technically be benchmarked at all, which makes the whole comparison invalid
That test set favors semantic matching by design, so results may not hold for exact-match queries
The risk only exists if fewer than 1000 documents were used in the test
questions.explain: Benchmark results are workload-dependent. A paraphrase-heavy set favors dense retrieval by construction; exact-match-heavy workloads (codes, IDs) often favor BM25. Generalizing from one test set overstates the conclusion.

feedback.right: A paraphrase-heavy test set favours semantic matching, so it says little about exact-match queries.
feedback.wrong: The test set was built for semantic matching, so the result may not hold for exact-match queries like IDs or codes. One benchmark doesn't generalise.

questions.text: A validation node in a LangGraph workflow fails intermittently, and the team wants exactly one re-generation attempt, not an infinite loop, before surfacing an error. What must the state design include?
options: A retry counter in shared state that a conditional edge checks before routing back once
Nothing special is needed, since LangGraph automatically caps every loop at one iteration
Removing the retriever node entirely would also prevent any possible chance of looping
A global variable outside the graph, since state objects cannot hold counters
questions.explain: Safely bounding a retry loop requires an explicit counter within the shared state that the conditional edge logic checks, routing back once and then to error-handling, rather than relying on any implicit default limit.

feedback.right: A retry counter in state lets the conditional edge loop back exactly once, then route to error handling.
feedback.wrong: Keep a retry counter in shared state and have the conditional edge check it. LangGraph doesn't cap a loop at one pass for you, and state can hold counters.

questions.text: An architect is deciding whether to precompute a hybrid index offline or score both retrievers at query time, under tight latency and storage budgets. What best frames this decision?
options: It is purely a front-end display choice with no real backend performance implications at all
It trades query-time latency against the storage and upkeep cost of a fresh precomputed index
It depends only on whether the LLM supports function calling at all
Precomputing is always strictly worse than query-time scoring, regardless of scale
questions.explain: Precomputed hybrid indexes cut query-time latency but add storage and re-indexing/maintenance overhead; computing at query time avoids that overhead but costs more latency per request.

feedback.right: Precomputing makes queries faster but costs storage and re-indexing; scoring at query time is the reverse.
feedback.wrong: It's a trade-off between query-time latency and the storage and maintenance cost of a precomputed index. Neither option is always better.

questions.text: An engineer is unsure where query rewriting belongs. Placing it after retrieval instead of before would cause what specific problem?
