feedback.wrong: A BiLSTM uses two passes, forward and backward, to capture past and future context. It still uses embeddings, and a plain LSTM only sees past tokens.

questions.text: Correct the order of execution during a SQL Execution?
questions.explain: FROM → WHERE → SELECT is the order how it executes.

feedback.right: SQL logically runs FROM (pick the table), then WHERE (filter rows), then SELECT (choose columns).
feedback.wrong: The logical order is FROM, then WHERE, then SELECT. SELECT is written first but evaluated after the rows are chosen.

questions.text: A DataFrame has 1,000 partitions. You want to increase them to 2,000. Which operation should you use?

feedback.right: repartition() can increase or decrease partitions (with a full shuffle); coalesce() can only reduce them.
feedback.wrong: Use repartition(2000). coalesce only reduces partitions, so coalesce(2000) on 1,000 partitions does nothing.

questions.text: The key advantage of an RNN over a basic feed-forward ANN for sequence data is:
options: It can maintain a hidden state representing previous sequence information

feedback.right: An RNN carries a hidden state from step to step, which acts as memory of earlier inputs.
feedback.wrong: An RNN keeps a hidden state with information from previous steps. It still has parameters and needs training, and it handles variable-length input.

questions.text:
You have:

Orders table → 500 GB
Customer table → 5 MB

What is the Best optimization you would choose here?
questions.explain: Broadcast the smaller tables always than repartitioning it.

feedback.right: A 5 MB table fits on every executor, so broadcasting it avoids shuffling the 500 GB orders table.
feedback.wrong: Broadcast the customer table. Sending a 5 MB copy to every executor avoids shuffling 500 GB; repartitioning would shuffle both tables.

questions.text:
An order-service publishes order events to Kafka. A separate inventory-service needs to read those events and update stock.

Which component does inventory-service use?

feedback.right: Inventory-service reads events, so it's a consumer of the topic.
feedback.wrong: It's a Consumer. The order-service is the producer, and the topic and partition are where events are stored, not the reader.

questions.text:
Spark job generated 40,000 parquet files.

What is the best optimization before writing the data?
questions.explain: coalesce hels to reduce partition

feedback.right: coalesce() merges partitions without a full shuffle, so the job writes far fewer files.
feedback.wrong: Use coalesce() to reduce the number of partitions, and so the number of files, before writing. repartition(50000) would create even more files.

questions.text: Which method can reduce the number of partitions without performing a full shuffle?

feedback.right: coalesce() merges existing partitions on the same executors, so no full shuffle is needed.
feedback.wrong: Use coalesce(), which merges partitions without a full shuffle. repartition() always shuffles, even when reducing.

questions.text:
A data engineering team is processing a large customer dataset using PySpark. A developer wants to inspect the output of a DataFrame and considers using either collect() or show().

The developer says:

“I can use collect() to bring the entire result to my Python program, while show() is mainly used to display a small preview of the data.”

Which statement is TRUE?
options: collect() returns data to driver program
questions.explain: collect method returns data to driver.

feedback.right: collect() pulls every row back to the driver as a Python list, so use it only on small results. show() just prints a preview.
feedback.wrong: collect() returns all the data to the driver. show() only prints the first rows (20 by default) and returns None, not a list.

questions.text:
Spark inferred salary column as string and sometimes double.

What is the Best solution you would go with?
questions.explain: define schema explicitly is good choice and better comparung to infer and changing.

feedback.right: An explicit schema fixes the type up front, so salary is always the same type and Spark skips inference.
feedback.wrong: Define the schema explicitly. Inference can guess differently per file or sample; casting later patches the symptom after bad types have already crept in.

questions.text:
An ANN neuron has:

```
Inputs = [2, 3]
Weights = [0.5, 0.2]
Bias = 0.1
```

What is the pre-activation value?

feedback.right: Pre-activation is the weighted sum plus bias: 2×0.5 + 3×0.2 + 0.1 = 1.0 + 0.6 + 0.1 = 1.7.
feedback.wrong: It's 1.7: multiply each input by its weight, add them, then add the bias. 2×0.5 + 3×0.2 + 0.1 = 1.0 + 0.6 + 0.1.

questions.text:
A DataFrame requires 30 minutes to generate and is used 5 times.

Caching it:

memory usage = high
recomputation cost = very high

What should you evaluate?
options: Whether the repeated computation cost justifies storage/memory consumption

feedback.right: Caching is a trade-off: 30 minutes saved on each of 5 reuses versus the memory the cache takes up.
feedback.wrong: Weigh the recomputation cost against the memory used. A 30-minute job reused 5 times usually justifies caching, but never 'always' or 'never'.

questions.text:
Two tables:

```
A = 1 TB
B = 500 GB
```

Both are joined on customer_id.

One customer represents 40% of all records.

Increasing:

```
spark.sql.shuffle.partitions
```

from 200 to 2,000 does not necessarily solve the fundamental issue because:
options: The hot key can still concentrate records into a problematic partition

feedback.right: All rows for one key go to the same partition, so a key holding 40% of the data stays one giant partition however many you add.
feedback.wrong: One hot key still lands in a single partition however many partitions there are. Fix skew with salting or a skew-aware join instead.

questions.text:
A Spark job has 1,000 tasks.

The Spark UI shows:

990 tasks → completed in 20 seconds
10 tasks → running for 15 minutes

The developer discovers that a few customer IDs contain millions of records.

What is the likely cause?

feedback.right: A few tasks running far longer because a few keys hold millions of rows is data skew.
feedback.wrong: It's data skew: a few customer IDs make 10 tasks huge while the rest finish fast. Predicate pushdown and column pruning are optimisations, not causes of slowness.

questions.text: Which situation is most suitable for caching?
options: DataFrame is very small and never reused
Expensive DataFrame transformation is reused multiple times
DataFrame is immediately written and discarded

feedback.right: Cache when an expensive result is reused several times; that's when it pays for its memory.
feedback.wrong: Caching suits an expensive DataFrame that's reused several times. Caching something used once only costs memory and time.

questions.text: Which technique can be used to handle severe data skew?

feedback.right: Salting adds a random prefix to hot keys, spreading their rows over many partitions.
feedback.wrong: Use salting to spread hot keys across partitions. More driver memory or collecting data doesn't help the overloaded tasks on the executors.

questions.text: Which is BAD practice you would consider during spark processing?
options: All the above are bad practice.
questions.explain: Cache one-time used DataFrame

feedback.right: Caching data you only use once spends memory and time for no benefit.
feedback.wrong: Caching a DataFrame used only once is the bad practice. Caching reused DataFrames and small lookup tables is good practice.

questions.text:
Cluster:

50 cores available

Spark submit:

```
--num-executors 2
--executor-cores 2
```
Problem?
questions.explain: General calculation of total cores and remaining cluster capacity.

feedback.right: 2 executors × 2 cores = 4 of 50 cores used, so the cluster is badly underused.
feedback.wrong: The cluster is underutilised: 2 × 2 = 4 cores out of 50. Raise the executors or cores to use the capacity.

questions.text:
Consider:

```
df1 = expensive_transformation(df)

df1.count()
df1.groupBy("country").sum("sales")
df1.filter("sales > 1000").count()
```

Which optimization is potentially useful?
options: Cache the original raw DataFrame only

feedback.right: df1 is reused by three actions, so caching it avoids running the expensive transformation three times.
feedback.wrong: Cache df1, which three actions reuse; otherwise the expensive transformation reruns each time. Caching the raw data doesn't save that work.

questions.text:
A telecom company has 20,000 customer records with features such as age, monthly bill, contract type, tenure, and number of complaints. The data is mostly structured.

Which would be a reasonable first approach?
options: Traditional ML such as Random Forest or XGBoost

feedback.right: For structured, tabular data, tree ensembles like Random Forest or XGBoost are the standard strong baseline.
feedback.wrong: Start with traditional ML such as Random Forest or XGBoost. CNNs suit images, LSTMs sequences and GANs generation, none of which fits tabular data.

questions.text: A VNet has 10.0.1.0/24 (web) and 10.0.2.0/24 (database) subnets. Why separate them?
options: For security isolation and different NSG rules

feedback.right: Separate subnets let you apply different NSG rules, e.g. only the web subnet may reach the database.
feedback.wrong: Subnets are separated for security isolation, with different NSG rules per tier. It isn't about speed or cost, and Azure doesn't require it.

questions.text:
A developer has this image:

python:3.12

They run it three times.

How many containers can be created from the same image?

feedback.right: An image is a template; each docker run creates a new, independent container from it.
feedback.wrong: You can create as many containers as you like from one image. Each docker run starts a separate container from the same template.

questions.text: A customer says "My phone rang but the call dropped as soon as I picked up." Which call phase failed?

feedback.right: The call set up and rang fine, but failed the moment it was picked up, which is the answer phase.
feedback.wrong: The answer phase failed. Setup and ringing worked (the phone rang); the drop happened exactly when the call was answered.

questions.text: A Platinum SLA customer experiences 15 min of downtime in a month (SLA allows 4.3 min). What is the consequence?

feedback.right: 15 minutes is well over the 4.3 allowed, so the SLA is breached and penalties or service credits apply.
feedback.wrong: It's an SLA breach: 15 minutes against 4.3 allowed, which triggers a penalty or credit note. The customer isn't at fault.

questions.text: In VoLTE, which pair correctly matches signaling and media paths?

feedback.right: In VoLTE, SIP sets up and controls the call and RTP carries the actual voice.
feedback.wrong: Signaling is SIP and media is RTP. SS7 and TDM belong to legacy circuit-switched networks.

questions.text: A customer upgrades from 4G to 5G and sees latency drop from 50 ms to 5 ms. What is the PRIMARY reason?
options: Cloud-native SBA core + NR air interface

feedback.right: The 5G NR air interface and the cloud-native core (SBA) are what cut latency so sharply.
feedback.wrong: The drop comes from 5G's NR air interface and cloud-native SBA core. SIM size and antenna height don't affect latency.

questions.text: A CDR shows a 322-second call. Tariff is ₹1.00/min with rounding up to next minute. What is the charge?

feedback.right: 322 seconds is 5.37 minutes, rounded up to 6, and 6 × ₹1 = ₹6.
feedback.wrong: It's ₹6.00. 322 s is about 5.37 minutes, and the tariff rounds up to the next whole minute (6). ₹5.36 ignores the rounding rule.

questions.text: A user's second request shows X-Cache: EXPIRED instead of HIT. What is the MOST likely cause?

feedback.right: The cached copy outlived its 10-second TTL, so the edge marked it EXPIRED and revalidated with the origin.
feedback.wrong: EXPIRED means the cached copy's TTL (10 s) ran out between requests. The cache works fine; it just needed to refresh.

questions.text: A GenAI NOC summary says "~30 customers affected" but a PON can serve up to 128 ONTs. What is the AI's mistake?

feedback.right: A PON can serve up to 128 ONTs, so '~30 customers' likely understates how many were hit.
feedback.wrong: The AI under-estimated the impact. One PON can serve up to 128 ONTs, so far more than 30 customers could be affected.

questions.text: An engineer needs a VM accessible from the internet but without exposing it directly. What is the BEST approach?
options: Attach a public IP to the VM
Place VM in private subnet behind a Load Balancer

feedback.right: The VM stays in a private subnet and only the load balancer faces the internet.
feedback.wrong: Put the VM in a private subnet behind a load balancer. A public IP, open port 22 or no NSGs exposes it directly.

questions.text:
A containerized application listens on port 8080 inside the container:

Application → 8080

The developer runs:

```
docker run myapp
```

and tries:

http://localhost:8080

but cannot access it.

Which command would expose the port?

feedback.right: -p host:container publishes the container's port on the host, so localhost:8080 reaches the app.
feedback.wrong: Use docker run -p 8080:8080 myapp. Without -p the container port isn't published; docker port only shows existing mappings.

questions.text: A postpaid bill shows a "pro-rata charge" because the plan was activated on the 15th. What does this mean?
options: Charged for only part of the month

feedback.right: Pro-rata means charged in proportion: activated on the 15th, so only about half the month is billed.
feedback.wrong: Pro-rata means you're charged for only part of the month, from activation on the 15th. It isn't extra usage or a discount.

questions.text: A customer complains VoIP calls fail but internet browsing works fine. Which layer do you investigate FIRST?

feedback.right: Browsing works, so access and transport are fine. VoIP failing points to the service layer (e.g. the IMS/SIP platform).
feedback.wrong: Investigate the service network first. Browsing works, so the access and transport paths are fine; the voice service itself is the likely fault.

questions.text: A technician runs ping -c 4 google.com and gets replies with time=250 ms. Which QoS metric does this represent?

feedback.right: Ping round-trip time measures latency.
feedback.wrong: That's latency, the round-trip delay. Jitter is variation in delay, and packet loss would show as missing replies.

questions.text: A developer asks why TCP is used for web and UDP for VoIP. What is the correct reasoning?
options: TCP guarantees delivery/order; UDP favors speed

feedback.right: TCP guarantees delivery and order for web pages; UDP skips retransmission so voice stays real-time.
feedback.wrong: TCP guarantees delivery and order, while UDP favours speed, which suits real-time voice. Both use ports, and neither is tied to 5G.

questions.text:
An application requires different database URLs for development, testing, and production.

The developer currently hardcodes:

```
DB_URL = "mysql://dev-db:3306/app"
```

What is a better Docker approach?
options: Create a separate Docker Engine for each environment
Store configuration inside the Docker image
Create a new container for every configuration value

feedback.right: Environment variables let one image run in dev, test and prod with different settings.
feedback.wrong: Use environment variables (docker run -e or Compose env files). Baking config into the image means a rebuild for every environment.

questions.text: A telecom employee is asked to classify "customer complaint handling." Which is correct?

feedback.right: Complaint handling deals with customers, so it's BSS (Business Support Systems).
feedback.wrong: It's BSS, the customer-facing side: CRM, billing and complaints. OSS covers network operations.

questions.text:
A company currently uses fraud_model_v1 in production. A data scientist trains fraud_model_v2.

After deployment, the number of incorrect predictions increases significantly.

What should the team do first?
options: Investigate model performance and consider rolling back to the previous stable version

feedback.right: Check what went wrong and roll back to the stable v1 if needed. Keeping old versions makes that possible.
feedback.wrong: Investigate the performance and consider rolling back to v1. Deleting v1 or the training data removes your safety net.

questions.text: A CDN edge cache returns X-Cache: MISS. What does the edge do next?
options: Fetch from origin and cache it

feedback.right: On a MISS the edge fetches the content from the origin, serves it and caches it for later requests.
feedback.wrong: The edge fetches from the origin and caches the result. A MISS is normal and isn't an error.

questions.text: A GenAI tool drafts a customer care response but misses the customer's specific complaint. What is the MOST important next step?
options: Human review and edit before sending

feedback.right: A person should review and fix the draft before it reaches the customer.
feedback.wrong: Have a human review and edit the draft before sending. Sending it as-is ignores the complaint, and deleting it wastes the useful parts.

questions.text: A user reports "no internet, but calls work" on 4G. Where is the MOST likely issue?
options: Core network — user plane data path

feedback.right: Calls work but data doesn't, so the radio link is fine; the core's user-plane data path is the likely fault.
feedback.wrong: The core network's user-plane data path is the most likely issue. Calls prove the access network and phone work; the data path specifically is failing.

questions.text: A customer orders FTTH broadband. Which inventory layer holds "OLT port, VLAN, and IP address"?

feedback.right: OLT ports, VLANs and IP addresses are physical and logical network resources, so they live in resource inventory.
feedback.wrong: They're in Resource Inventory. Customer inventory holds customer details, and service inventory holds the services sold.

questions.text: A cloud-native OSS service needs updating without affecting others. What is the BEST approach?
options: Deploy micro service independently via CI/CD

feedback.right: Microservices can be deployed independently through CI/CD without touching the rest of the system.
feedback.wrong: Deploy the microservice independently through CI/CD. Updating a whole monolith or shutting down affects every other service.

questions.text: A prepaid customer makes calls with ₹0 balance. Which system is likely malfunctioning?

feedback.right: The Online Charging System checks prepaid balance in real time; calls at ₹0 mean it isn't blocking them.
feedback.wrong: The OCS is malfunctioning. It checks prepaid balance in real time and should block calls at ₹0. Billing is the postpaid, after-the-fact system.

questions.text: A data center uses 200 kW total power and 150 kW for IT equipment. What is the PUE?

feedback.right: PUE = total facility power / IT power = 200 / 150 = 1.33.
feedback.wrong: PUE is total power divided by IT power: 200 / 150 = 1.33. 0.75 is the ratio upside down; PUE can never be below 1.

questions.text: The priority is reducing customer-facing effort. Between a chatbot and an NOC alarm summarizer, which do you pick?

feedback.right: A customer care chatbot directly cuts the effort customers spend. The NOC summarizer helps internal staff.
feedback.wrong: Pick the customer care chatbot, since the goal is less effort for customers. The NOC alarm summarizer helps engineers, not customers.

questions.text: A NOC receives 500 alarms in 2 minutes. What should the engineer do FIRST?
options: Correlate alarms to find root cause

feedback.right: Correlating alarms finds the one root cause behind the flood, instead of chasing 500 symptoms.
feedback.wrong: Correlate the alarms first to find the root cause. Restarting everything or closing tickets without a diagnosis can make things worse.

questions.text: A NOC engineer sees alarms from "gNB-DEL-01" and "AMF-MUM-01." Which generation is this?

feedback.right: gNB (the 5G base station) and AMF (the 5G core access function) are both 5G network elements.
feedback.wrong: It's 5G: gNB is the 5G base station and AMF is part of the 5G core. In 4G these would be eNodeB and MME.

questions.text: A company receives new labeled customer data every month. The team wants the model to automatically retrain when sufficient new data becomes available.

feedback.right: An automated retraining pipeline retrains on new data when enough arrives, with no manual steps.
feedback.wrong: Build an automated retraining pipeline triggered by new data. Deleting the model or editing predictions by hand doesn't scale.

questions.text: In a Docker mini-DC lab, docker run -d --name origin nginx is executed. What does origin represent?
options: The source of truth for content

feedback.right: The nginx container named origin plays the origin server, the source of truth that edge caches fetch from.
feedback.wrong: origin is the origin server, the source of truth for the content. Edge caches fetch from it; it isn't the firewall, client or DNS.
